- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- blog-post: Use when writing or editing a post for the Cordango marketing blog (marketing/blog/posts/). Triggers include "write a blog post", "new post for the cordango blog", "draft a post about X", "introduce <feature> on the blog". Enforces the house writing conventions (anti-AI-tell guardrails, no em-dashes), the frontmatter contract, the OpenArt blueprint hero workflow, and the German (Sie-form) translation step.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.description: Map the source generator architecture
input.prompt:
Explore the repository at c:\Work\github\AppBuilder, specifically the OSS submodule at `oss/cordango`. I need a thorough map of the source generation / standalone scaffold architecture.

Focus on:
1. The `oss/cordango/src/` directory tree — list every project and its purpose (especially anything named Standalone, Generator, Compiler, CLI).
2. The "SourceGen" / generator entry point: where does code generation start? What is the top-level abstraction (interfaces, base classes) for a generator/target? Find files like `*Generator*.cs`, `IGenerator`, `ITargetGenerator`, etc.
3. How the DotNet+Vue target is currently structured: which files emit C# (entities, EF config, controllers, roles, commands, migrations) vs which files emit Vue (screens, components). Are backend and frontend emission already separated into distinct classes/folders, or interleaved?
4. Templates: where do scaffold templates live (e.g. a `templates/` folder, embedded resources, or `.csproj` content includes)? How are they materialized?
5. How the CLI invokes generation — command names, flags (e.g. `--allow-incomplete`), any notion of a "target" or "stack" selection.
6. What the input model is: the AppDefinition / IR that generators consume. Where is it defined and what shape does it have (entities, screens, workflows, computed, guards, permissions, commands, roles)?

Report file paths with line numbers for key abstractions. Be very thorough — this determines how a second language target would plug in. Report back a structured map, not raw file dumps.

Report exact file paths with line numbers. Be very thorough.

6	using System.Text.Json.Nodes;
7	
8	namespace Cordango.SourceGen;
9	
10	/// <summary>Which compiler produced an artifact, recorded so a generated repository can say what
11	/// built it years later.</summary>
12	public sealed record CompilerInfo(string Id, string Version);
13	
14	/// <summary>
15	/// ONE canonical input, and the reason it is one thing rather than two.
16	///
17	/// <para>A generator needs the definition (what the author wrote) and the manifest (what the
18	/// compiler derived from it: canonicalised processes, synthesised commands, base fields, default
19	/// views). Handing those over as two parameters invites a caller to supply a definition and a
20	/// manifest that do not describe the same application — which is exactly the "which representation
21	/// is truth?" problem the App Definition exists to avoid, reintroduced at the last possible
22	/// moment.</para>
23	///
24	/// <para>So they travel as a pair, produced together by one compile. This is not a new intermediate
25	/// representation: every field here already existed as an output of the existing pipeline. The type
26	/// only makes a mismatched pair impossible to express.</para>
27	/// </summary>
28	/// <param name="Definition">The App Definition after deterministic fills — the artifact
29	/// <paramref name="DefinitionHash"/> covers.</param>
30	/// <param name="Manifest">What the compiler derived. A generator reads process/command/field facts
31	/// from HERE rather than re-deriving them, so it cannot disagree with the runtime about what the
32	/// definition meant.</param>
33	public sealed record CompiledAppArtifact(
34	    JsonObject Definition,
35	    JsonObject Manifest,
36	    string DefinitionHash,
37	    CompilerInfo Compiler);
38	
39	/// <summary>What the CLI asks a generator to produce.</summary>
40	/// <param name="Options">Target-specific switches (seed value, locales, partial-UI). Deliberately
41	/// untyped: the SDK does not get a vote on what a generator needs to be told.</param>
42	public sealed record GenerateRequest(CompiledAppArtifact App, JsonObject Options)
43	{
44	    public static GenerateRequest For(CompiledAppArtifact app) => new(app, new JsonObject());
45	
46	    /// <summary>A string option, or null. Reading options through one accessor keeps a generator
47	    /// from inventing three spellings of "is it there".</summary>
48	    public string? Option(string name) =>
49	        Options[name] is JsonValue v && v.TryGetValue<string>(out var s) ? s : null;
50	
51	    public bool Flag(string name) =>
52	        Options[name] is JsonValue v && v.TryGetValue<bool>(out var b) && b;
53	}
54	
55	/// <summary>
56	/// One file a generator wants written.
57	///
58	/// <para><paramref name="RelativePath"/> is forward-slashed and relative to the output root. It is
59	/// NOT a path the generator writes to — the runner owns the filesystem, so a generator cannot
60	/// escape the output directory, cannot leave a half-written tree behind, and cannot make two runs
61	/// differ by writing in a different order.</para>
62	/// </summary>
63	public sealed record GeneratedFile(string RelativePath, string Content);
64	
65	/// <summary>Something a target has to say about a definition it was asked to build.</summary>
66	/// <param name="Code">A stable <c>CORD21xx</c> identifier. Codes exist so a person can search for
67	/// one and a script can branch on one without reading English.</param>
68	/// <param name="JsonPath">Where in the definition, e.g. <c>$.entities[2].fields[7]</c>. A capability
69	/// message without a location is a puzzle rather than a report.</param>
70	public sealed record Diagnostic(string Code, string Message, string? JsonPath = null)
71	{
72	    public override string ToString() =>
73	        JsonPath is null ? $"{Code}: {Message}" : $"{Code}: {Message} ({JsonPath})";
74	}
75	
76	/// <summary>What a generator answered.</summary>
77	/// <param name="Errors">Non-empty means nothing is written. A generator reports EVERY reason it can
78	/// find rather than the first, because a person fixing an app wants the list.</param>
79	public sealed record GenerateResult(
80	    IReadOnlyList<GeneratedFile> Files,
81	    IReadOnlyList<Diagnostic> Warnings,
82	    IReadOnlyList<Diagnostic> Errors)
83	{
84	    public bool Ok => Errors.Count == 0;
85	
86	    public static GenerateResult Failed(params Diagnostic[] errors) => new([], [], errors);
87	
88	    public static GenerateResult Produced(
89	        IReadOnlyList<GeneratedFile> files, IReadOnlyList<Diagnostic>? warnings = null) =>
90	        new(files, warnings ?? [], []);
91	}
92	
93	/// <summary>
94	/// A source generator for one target stack.
95	///
96	/// <para>It receives a compiled application and returns files. It does not know about YAML, about
97	/// workspaces, about a Cordango server, or about where its output will land — the CLI owns all of
98	/// that. The narrowness is the point: it is the same surface an out-of-process generator written in
99	/// another language gets over stdin and stdout.</para>
100	/// </summary>
101	public interface IAppSourceGenerator
102	{
103	    /// <summary>Stable identifier, e.g. <c>dotnet-vue</c>. This is what <c>--target</c> names.</summary>
104	    string Id { get; }
105	
106	    /// <summary>Semantic version of the GENERATOR, recorded in the build metadata. Two runs of the
107	    /// same version on the same definition must produce the same bytes.</summary>
108	    string Version { get; }
109	
110	    /// <summary>What this target can and cannot express. Answerable without generating anything, so
111	    /// <c>cordango check --target</c> costs nothing.</summary>
112	    GeneratorCapabilities Capabilities { get; }
113	
114	    GenerateResult Generate(GenerateRequest request);
115	}

See LICENSE in the repository root. 5 6 namespace Cordango.SourceGen; 7 8 /// 9 /// One axis of the vocabulary, split into what a target builds and what it deliberately does not. 10 /// 11 /// Withheld carries a REASON, and that is the whole design. A capability model that 12 /// only lists what works answers "no" and stops. Somebody then reads the schema, sees the feature is 13 /// legal, and cannot tell whether the target forgot it, rejected it on purpose, or has it planned. 14 /// The reason turns a refusal into an explanation, and it is the same doctrine 15 /// CordWordMap.Withheld already applies to the authoring vocabulary. 16 /// 17 /// It is also checkable: a test asserts that supported ∪ withheld covers everything the schema 18 /// allows, so a value added to the language cannot be quietly unhandled by a target that claims to 19 /// know its own limits. 20 /// 21 /// What to say about a value that is not in either list. Most axes are 22 /// closed vocabularies where that cannot happen; the open one is targetApp, where the value 23 /// is another application's key and could be anything. A target that knows why it can never resolve 24 /// one says so once here rather than leaving the validator to invent wording per call site. 25 public sealed record CapabilitySet( 26 IReadOnlySet Supported, 27 IReadOnlyDictionary Withheld, 28 string? Fallback = null) 29 { 30 public static CapabilitySet Of( 31 IEnumerable supported, string? fallback = null, 32 params (string Value, string Why)[] withheld) => 33 new(supported.ToHashSet(StringComparer.Ordinal), 34 withheld.ToDictionary(w => w.Value, w => w.Why, StringComparer.Ordinal), 35 fallback); 36 37 public bool Allows(string value) => Supported.Contains(value); 38 39 /// Why a value is not built, or null when the target has never heard of it. The two are 40 /// different answers and a message should not blur them. 41 public string? WhyNot(string value) => Withheld.TryGetValue(value, out var why) ? why : null; 42 43 /// The message a diagnostic carries: the documented reason where there is one, the 44 /// target's standing explanation where the value is outside any list it could enumerate, and an 45 /// honest last resort otherwise. 46 public string Explain(string value) => 47 WhyNot(value) ?? Fallback ?? $"'{value}' is not something this target knows how to build"; 48 49 public IReadOnlySet Known => 50 Supported.Concat(Withheld.Keys).ToHashSet(StringComparer.Ordinal); 51 } 52 53 /// 54 /// What a target can build, declared as data so that cordango check --target can answer 55 /// without generating anything — and so an out-of-process generator can answer the same question 56 /// over stdout. 57 /// 58 /// Block kinds. The largest axis and the one most likely to be partial. 59 /// Effect types a command or workflow may run. 60 /// Workflow trigger events. 61 /// Field types the target can store and render. 62 /// Values of targetApp the target can resolve — for a 63 /// standalone application, the platform apps it carries a local equivalent of. Anything else is a 64 /// reference into a separately installed application and cannot be resolved at all. 65 /// Values of targetEntity within those, same argument. 66 /// Ordered series and prev(): a row whose value depends on the 67 /// row before it. 68 /// Rollups with a window or match, i.e. aggregation that 69 /// is not simply "up the parent reference". 70 public sealed record GeneratorCapabilities( 71 CapabilitySet Blocks, 72 CapabilitySet Effects, 73 CapabilitySet Triggers, 74 CapabilitySet FieldTypes, 75 CapabilitySet PlatformTargets, 76 CapabilitySet PlatformEntities, 77 bool SeriesAndPrev, 78 bool WindowedRollups); 79

See LICENSE in the repository root. 5 6 using System.Text.Json.Nodes; 7 using Cordango.SourceGen.DotNetVue.Emit; 8 using Cordango.SourceGen.DotNetVue.Model; 9 10 namespace Cordango.SourceGen.DotNetVue; 11 12 /// 13 /// The standalone target: one application, as conventional source you own. 14 /// 15 /// ASP.NET Core with MVC controllers, EF Core against PostgreSQL, ASP.NET Core Identity for 16 /// sign-in, Vue 3 and Vuetify on the front. Nothing about the generated result depends on Cordango 17 /// at runtime: no licence check, no account, no model API, no phone home. It keeps working if this 18 /// project stops existing. 19 /// 20 /// Its capabilities are declared before its emitters exist, and that is deliberate. 21 /// A target is two separable things — a claim about what it can build, and the code that builds it — 22 /// and the claim is what cordango check --target needs. Publishing it first means a person 23 /// can find out today whether their application is compatible, and it means the capability list is 24 /// written from the language rather than backwards from whatever the emitters happened to 25 /// implement. 26 /// 27 public sealed class DotNetVueGenerator : IAppSourceGenerator 28 { 29 public string Id => "dotnet-vue"; 30 31 /// Zero major: the emitters are not written. The version is in the build metadata of 32 /// everything this produces, so it starts honest rather than starting at 1.0. 33 public string Version => BuildVersion.Current; 34 35 public GeneratorCapabilities Capabilities { get; } = new( 36 // Every screen the language has, except the two that are ABOUT other applications. A 37 // standalone application can be large and can be complicated; what it cannot be is plural. 38 Blocks: CapabilitySet.Of( 39 [ 40 // Layout and text. 41 "section", "row", "columns", "stack", "grid", "card", "tabs", "split", "text", 42 // Records and fields. 43 "fields", "field", "cell", "chip", "avatar", "form", "hub", "settings", "repeat", 44 // Collections. 45 "view", "table", "board", "calendar", "child", 46 // Figures. 47 "stat", "tiles", "chart", "progress", "widgets", 48 // Behaviour. 49 "process", "action", "create", "control", "filterbar", 50 // Time and structure. 51 "gantt", "timeline", "orgchart", 52 // Forms. 53 "intake", "answers", 54 // Anything else a page can hold. 55 "externalEmbed", 56 ], 57 withheld: 58 [ 59 // EVERY refusal on this target is a platform capability, and every message says so 60 // the same way: name the feature, say what the platform does with it, say what a 61 // standalone application has instead, and give both ways forward. An earlier draft 62 // argued that related-apps was different in kind because the question is 63 // unanswerable with one application rather than merely unimplemented. True, and 64 // useless to a reader: from their side both are "the platform does this and this 65 // build does not", and cross-application data is the thing the platform is FOR. 66 ("history", 67 "record history is a Cordango Platform feature. The platform keeps a field-level " 68 + "audit trail for every record automatically (what changed, who changed it, and " 69 + "the value before and after), and this block is the screen that shows it. A " 70 + "standalone application keeps technical logs but no business audit trail, so " 71 + "there is nothing behind the block to render. Remove the block to build " 72 + "standalone, or run this application on Cordango Platform, where the trail is " 73 + "kept for you with nothing to configure"), 74 ("relatedApps", 75 "related apps is a Cordango Platform feature. On the platform every application " 76 + "shares one set of People and Organizations, so this block can show the deals, " 77 + "tickets and projects from across the company that point at this record. A " 78 + "standalone application has its own local People and Organizations and nothing " 79 + "installed beside it, so there is nothing for the block to look through. Remove " 80 + "the block to build standalone, or run this application on Cordango Platform"), 81 ]), 82 83 Effects: CapabilitySet.Of( 84 ["createRecord", "updateRecord", "createForEach", "notify", "email", "webhook"], 85 withheld: 86 [ 87 ("enrich", 88 "enrichment is a Cordango Platform feature. The platform researches a company " 89 + "from its own website and files what it finds against your Organizations with " 90 + "the evidence attached. A standalone application ships with no model and no " 91 + "research pipeline, and is not meant to call one. Remove the effect to build " 92 + "standalone, or run this application on Cordango Platform"), 93 ]), 94 95 // Every trigger the language has. A standalone application runs its own background service 96 // for the scheduled ones rather than borrowing a platform scheduler. 97 Triggers: CapabilitySet.Of( 98 ["record.created", "record.updated", "record.deleted", "field.changed", "schedule"]), 99 100 // Every field type, including attachment: a generated application stores uploads on its own 101 // disk rather than in platform media storage. 102 FieldTypes: CapabilitySet.Of( 103 [ 104 "text", "longtext", "email", "url", "phone", "select", "multiselect", "boolean", 105 "integer", "decimal", "money", "date", "datetime", "reference", "attachment", "json", 106 ]), 107 108 // The platform primitives a standalone build carries a local equivalent of. Anything else 109 // named by `targetApp` is a separately installed application, which cannot exist here. 110 PlatformTargets: CapabilitySet.Of( 111 ["platform", "core_organizations"], 112 fallback: 113 "references between applications are a Cordango Platform feature. The platform runs " 114 + "several applications on one shared company graph, so a record in one can point at a " 115 + "record in another. A standalone build is a single application: it carries its own " 116 + "People, Organizations, Departments and Groups and can reference those, but there is " 117 + "no second application for this field to resolve against. Point the field at a local " 118 + "entity to build standalone, or run this application on Cordango Platform"), 119 120 PlatformEntities: CapabilitySet.Of( 121 ["person", "department", "group", "organization", "contact"], 122 fallback: 123 "a standalone application carries local People, Organizations, Departments and Groups. " 124 + "Platform entities beyond those have nothing local to map onto, so this reference " 125 + "would have nowhere to point. Use one of the local entities to build standalone, or " 126 + "run this application on Cordango Platform"), 127 128 // An ordered series, where each row reads the one before it. The EXPRESSIONS are already 129 // shared — `ComputedExpr` parses and evaluates with one implementation — so what this 130 // commits to is the RECOMPUTE CASCADE: working out which records a write disturbs, in what 131 // order, without recomputing the world. That is the hardest thing in the platform runtime 132 // and it took two passes to make fast there. It is in scope because the alternative is a 133 // standalone target that cannot build the Budget Planner, and a calculation plane that only 134 // works on the hosted product is not the calculation plane being sold. 135 SeriesAndPrev: true, 136 137 // Rollups up a reference are a GROUP BY. Windowed and matched rollups are a declarative 138 // SUMIFS over a range or across siblings, and they lean on the same cascade. 139 WindowedRollups: true); 140 141 /// 142 /// The application, as files. 143 /// 144 /// Three layers, in this order: the SCAFFOLD (everything an application has before it has 145 /// any entities — host, sign-in, directory, packaging, the runtime as source), the BACKEND 146 /// (one class, one EF configuration, one descriptor and one controller per entity, plus the 147 /// compiled permission rules and the first migration), and the FRONT END (one page per screen, 148 /// a typed client, the router). Later layers overwrite earlier ones by path, which is how the 149 /// generated AppDbContext replaces the scaffold's empty one instead of colliding with 150 /// it. 151 /// 152 public GenerateResult Generate(GenerateRequest request) 153 { 154 ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(request); 155 156 var app = AppModel.From(request.App); 157 var allowIncomplete = request.Options?["allowIncomplete"]?.GetValue() ?? false; 158 var runtimeAsPackage = request.Options?["runtimeAsPackage"]?.GetValue() ?? false; 159 160 // The capability gate, and it does NOT stop the build. 161 // 162 // It used to. One `history` block on one screen refused an entire application — every entity, 163 // every workflow, every screen — because of a card on one page. That ratio is indefensible: 164 // the definition is valid, the ninety per cent this target CAN build is worth having, and the 165 // person can decide whether the missing tenth matters to them. 166 // 167 // So a capability this target lacks is reported and the thing is left out: a block becomes a 168 // card saying so, an effect does not fire, a reference to another application's record stays 169 // an unresolved id. Nothing is silently dropped, and the build still refuses by default — 170 // `--allow-incomplete` is how somebody says they know — but what they are refusing is now a 171 // list they can read rather than a wall. 172 // 173 // Block kinds are dropped from this list because the web emitter reports them itself, with 174 // the same codes and a path pointing at the page it actually rendered. Two entries for one 175 // card, one of them saying "not yet" about something that will never come, is worse than 176 // either alone. 177 var unsupported = TargetValidator.Validate(request.App.Definition, Capabilities) 178 .Where(d => d.Code is not (DiagnosticCodes.HistoryBlock 179 or DiagnosticCodes.RelatedAppsBlock 180 or DiagnosticCodes.UnsupportedBlock)) 181 .ToList(); 182 183 var files = new Dictionary(StringComparer.Ordinal); 184 var warnings = new List(); 185 186 void Add(GeneratedFile file) => files[file.RelativePath] = file; 187 188 var scaffold = new ScaffoldOptions(app.Name, app.Key, app.Namespace, RuntimeAsPackage: runtimeAsPackage); 189 foreach (var file in Scaffold.Files(scaffold)) Add(file); 190 191 Add(BackendEmitter.DbContext(app)); 192 Add(BackendEmitter.Descriptors(app)); 193 Add(BackendEmitter.Setup(app)); 194 Add(BackendEmitter.Permissions(app)); 195 Add(BackendEmitter.Commands(app)); 196 Add(WorkflowEmitter.Workflows(app)); 197 198 foreach (var entity in app.Entities) 199 { 200 Add(EntityEmitter.Emit(app, entity)); 201 Add(ConfigurationEmitter.Emit(app, entity)); 202 Add(BackendEmitter.Controller(app, entity)); 203 } 204 205 foreach (var file in MigrationEmitter.Emit(app)) Add(file); 206 207 foreach (var entity in app.Entities) 208 if (BackendEmitter.AutoFields(app, entity) is { } hook) 209 Add(hook); 210 211 // A dataset to open the application on. Derived from the seed alone, so two builds of the 212 // same definition produce the same rows. 213 Add(SeedEmitter.Emit(app, request.Options?["seed"]?.GetValue() ?? 42)); 214 215 var web = WebEmitter.Emit(app, allowIncomplete, Capabilities); 216 foreach (var file in web.Files) Add(file); 217 warnings.AddRange(web.Warnings); 218 219 // Everything this build could not do: what the target will never do, what the emitters have 220 // not got to yet, and the screens that fall into either. One list to decide whether the build 221 // needs permission; two lists in the README, because "not supported" and "not yet" are 222 // different news for whoever inherits the application. 223 var incomplete = new List([.. unsupported, .. web.Unsupported, .. NotYetEmitted(app)]); 224 225 if (!allowIncomplete && incomplete.Count > 0) 226 return GenerateResult.Failed([.. incomplete]); 227 228 warnings.AddRange(incomplete); 229 230 // Re-run the README with the scar, now that it is known whether there is one. 231 if (incomplete.Count > 0) 232 { 233 var scar = PartialBuildSection(incomplete); 234 foreach (var file in Scaffold.Files(scaffold with { PartialBuildSection = scar })) 235 if (file.RelativePath == "README.md") 236 Add(file); 237 } 238 239 return new GenerateResult( 240 [.. files.Values.OrderBy(f => f.RelativePath, StringComparer.Ordinal)], 241 warnings, 242 []); 243 } 244 245 /// 246 /// What the definition asks for that the emitters do not produce yet. 247 /// 248 /// Reported, never skipped. These are the gaps that would otherwise be invisible: 249 /// an application whose screens all render and whose approvals silently send no notification 250 /// looks finished, and the person testing it has no reason to suspect otherwise. A missing 251 /// screen at least leaves a hole. 252 /// 253 /// The capability declaration says this target SUPPORTS all of these, and that stays true: 254 /// a capability is a claim about the target, and these are the emitters catching up to it. When 255 /// they do, the diagnostics disappear on their own. 256 /// 257 private static IEnumerable NotYetEmitted(AppModel app) 258 { 259 for (var i = 0; i < app.Workflows.Count; i++) 260 { 261 var workflow = app.Workflows[i]; 262 var key = Model.AppModel.Str(workflow["key"]) 263 ?? i.ToString(System.Globalization.CultureInfo.InvariantCulture); 264 265 var trigger = workflow["trigger"] as JsonObject; 266 var @event = Model.AppModel.Str(trigger?["event"]); 267 268 // A trigger this target does not wire. `schedule` needs a host that is awake and a timer 269 // to wake it, which is a different piece of machinery from a hook on a write. 270 if (@event is null || !Emit.WorkflowEmitter.Triggers.Contains(@event)) 271 { 272 yield return new Diagnostic("CORD2302", 273 $"the workflow '{key}' triggers on '{@event ?? "nothing"}', which is not wired yet, " 274 + "so nothing will run.", 275 $"$.workflows[{i}].trigger"); 276 continue; 277 } 278 279 // A guard that cannot be written would make the workflow fire in cases the definition 280 // excludes — the same hazard as a command's guard, and louder here because a workflow 281 // runs without anybody watching. 282 if (!Emit.ConditionEmitter.TryEmit(workflow["when"], out _)) 283 yield return new Diagnostic("CORD2306", 284 $"the workflow '{key}' has a condition this generator cannot write, so it would " 285 + "run in cases the definition excludes.", 286 $"$.workflows[{i}].when"); 287 288 var unwritten = Model.AppModel.Arr(workflow["effects"]).OfType() 289 .Select(e => Model.AppModel.Str(e["type"])) 290 .Where(type => type is null || !Emit.WorkflowEmitter.Emitted.Contains(type)) 291 .Select(type => type ?? "an unnamed effect") 292 .Distinct(StringComparer.Ordinal) 293 .ToList(); 294 295 if (unwritten.Count > 0) 296 yield return new Diagnostic("CORD2303", 297 $"the workflow '{key}' declares {string.Join(" and ", unwritten)} effect(s), which are " 298 + "not generated yet. Its trigger fires and its other effects run; these do not.", 299 $"$.workflows[{i}].effects"); 300 } 301 302 foreach (var command in app.Commands) 303 { 304 // `notify` IS generated — it writes an in-app notification, which needs no mail server 305 // and no outbound network. The rest do, and an application that silently sent nothing 306 // would look like one whose emails were being swallowed. 307 var unsent = command.Effects 308 .Select(e => Model.AppModel.Str(e["type"])) 309 .Where(type => type is not null and not "notify") 310 .Distinct(StringComparer.Ordinal) 311 .ToList(); 312 313 if (unsent.Count > 0) 314 yield return new Diagnostic("CORD2303", 315 $"'{command.Label}' declares {string.Join(" and ", unsent)} effect(s), which are not " 316 + "generated yet. The command runs and moves the record; those effects do not fire. " 317 + "Its notify effects DO.", 318 $"$.commands[?(@.key=='{command.Key}')].effects"); 319 320 // A guard the emitter cannot write must not become an application without one. The 321 // command would run, look correct, and be more permissive than the definition — the 322 // only kind of generator bug that is invisible in the output. 323 if (!Emit.ConditionEmitter.TryEmit(command.Json["when"], out _)) 324 yield return new Diagnostic("CORD2306", 325 $"'{command.Label}' has a guard this generator cannot write, so the command would " 326 + "be generated WITHOUT it and would run in cases the definition refuses.", 327 $"$.commands[?(@.key=='{command.Key}')].when"); 328 } 329 330 foreach (var entity in app.Entities) 331 foreach (var field in entity.AuthoredFields.Where(f => f.Computed is not null)) 332 yield return new Diagnostic("CORD2305", 333 $"'{entity.Label}.{field.Label}' is computed, and the calculation is not generated yet. " 334 + "The column exists and stays empty.", 335 $"$.entities[?(@.key=='{entity.Key}')].fields[?(@.key=='{field.Key}')].computed"); 336 } 337 338 /// 339 /// The permanent mark a knowingly incomplete build leaves on the application it produced. 340 /// 341 /// In the README as well as in cordango.build.json, because the metadata is read by 342 /// tools and the README is read by people — and the person who inherits this repository in a 343 /// year is the one who needs to know that some screens were never generated. 344 /// 345 private static string PartialBuildSection(IReadOnlyList unsupported) 346 { 347 // CORD21xx is "this target cannot", CORD23xx is "these emitters do not yet". Separated 348 // because they are different news: one is a decision somebody should make about which 349 // product they want, and the other goes away on its own in a later release. 9	namespace Cordango.Cli.Generate;

11	/// <summary>
12	/// Which generators this build of the CLI can reach, and what <c>--target</c> may name.
13	///
14	/// <para>The registry lives HERE rather than in the SDK on purpose: the SDK defines what a generator
15	/// is and must not know that any particular one exists, or the first-party target becomes a special
16	/// case that every other target is measured against. The CLI is the composition root, so this is
17	/// the one place that knows the list.</para>
18	///
19	/// <para>An out-of-process generator — an executable that answers the protocol over stdin and
20	/// stdout — joins by being resolvable here too. Nothing above this class will need to change.</para>
21	/// </summary>
22	public static class Targets
23	{
24	    private static readonly IAppSourceGenerator[] Registered = [new DotNetVueGenerator()];
25	
26	    /// <summary>
27	    /// What a user writes versus what a generator calls itself.
28	    ///
29	    /// <para><c>standalone</c> is the word for the IDEA — one application, yours, deployable
30	    /// anywhere — and <c>dotnet-vue</c> is one implementation of it. Somebody who wants a standalone
31	    /// application should not have to know which stack is the default one, and the day a second
32	    /// certified target exists, this alias is where the default is stated rather than a thing every
33	    /// user has to relearn.</para>
34	    /// </summary>
35	    private static readonly IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> Aliases =
36	        new Dictionary<string, string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
37	        {
38	            ["standalone"] = "dotnet-vue",
39	        };
40	
41	    public static IEnumerable<IAppSourceGenerator> All => Registered;
42	
43	    public static IAppSourceGenerator? Find(string target)
44	    {
45	        var id = Aliases.TryGetValue(target, out var aliased) ? aliased : target;
46	        return Registered.FirstOrDefault(g => string.Equals(g.Id, id, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase));
47	    }
48	
49	    /// <summary>Every name that resolves, for an error message that lists the alternatives instead
50	    /// of leaving somebody to guess the spelling.</summary>
51	    public static string Known =>
52	        string.Join(", ", Registered.Select(g => g.Id).Concat(Aliases.Keys).OrderBy(n => n, StringComparer.Ordinal));
53	}

1	// The one way this application talks to its server.
2	//
3	// Everything goes through here so that three things are decided once instead of at every call site:
4	// the session cookie is sent, the antiforgery token is echoed on anything that changes state, and an
5	// error comes back as an object with a stable `code` rather than as a thrown string.
6	
7	/** Read a cookie by name. The antiforgery token arrives as one, deliberately readable by script on
8	 *  this origin and by nothing else — which is the entire mechanism. */
9	function cookie(name) {
10	  const match = document.cookie.match(new RegExp('(^|; )' + name + '=([^;]*)'))
11	  return match ? decodeURIComponent(match[2]) : null
12	}

15	export class ApiError extends Error {
16	  constructor(status, body) {
17	    super(body?.error || `Request failed (${status})`)
18	    this.name = 'ApiError'
19	    this.status = status
20	    this.code = body?.code || 'server.error'
21	    this.fields = body?.fields || []
22	  }
23	}

25	const UNSAFE = new Set(['POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'])
26	
27	async function request(method, path, body, options = {}) {
28	  const headers = { Accept: 'application/json', ...options.headers }
29	
30	  // Every state-changing request carries the token. The server enforces this globally rather than
31	  // per endpoint, so forgetting it here fails loudly on the first attempt instead of leaving one
32	  // quiet hole in an otherwise protected surface.

1	# What the standalone scaffold takes from TCDev.APIGenerator
2	
3	Cordango's standalone target generates a conventional ASP.NET Core application. The question this
4	document answers, once, is how much of that application should be *generated per entity* and how
5	much should be *written once and shared* — and whether an existing answer to that question could be
6	adopted rather than rewritten.
7	
8	The existing answer assessed here is [DeeJayTC/net-dynamic-api][repo] (`TCDev.APIGenerator`), read at
9	commit `4279e35`, February 2023, .NET 6. It solves a neighbouring problem: turn annotated POCOs into
10	a REST API at runtime. Verdicts below are **adopt** (take the package as a dependency), **absorb**
11	(lift the code), or **pattern** (take the idea, write our own).
12	
13	[repo]: https://github.com/DeeJayTC/net-dynamic-api
14	
15	## The verdict in one line
16	
17	**Pattern, throughout. Nothing is adopted as a dependency and nothing is lifted verbatim.** The
18	shape of the thing — generic machinery once, thin types per entity — is exactly right and is the
19	architecture of `Cordango.Standalone`. The mechanism underneath it is built for a problem we do not
20	have, and the code carries defects a generator would replicate into every application it produced.
21	
22	## Why not adopt the package
23	
24	The library targets .NET 6 and its last release is `0.7.1-rc1`. It pulls in Swashbuckle,
25	Newtonsoft.Json, EntityFramework.Triggers and `EFCore.AutomaticMigrations` transitively, and its
26	optional modules add OData, GraphQL and RabbitMQ. A generated Cordango application should have a
27	dependency list its owner can read in one screen and audit themselves; inheriting a stack to get one
28	generic controller inverts that.
29	
30	The deeper reason is the one below.
31	
32	## The mechanism we do not need
33	
34	`TCDev.APIGenerator` discovers its entities **at runtime, by reflection**: `AddAssembly` scans for
35	`[Api]`, `GenericTypeControllerFeatureProvider` closes `GenericController<T,TId>` over each
36	discovered type, `GenericControllerRouteConvention` rewrites the route from the attribute, and
37	`GenericDbContext.OnModelCreating` calls `ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly` plus `builder.Entity(t)`
38	for whatever else it found.
39	
40	That machinery exists to answer a question at startup that **we answer at generation time**. We know
41	every entity, every route and every key type when we emit the code. Reflection buys us nothing there
42	and costs three things that matter for a generated artifact:
43	
44	- **Determinism.** Registration order becomes assembly-scan order. The whole build contract is that
45	  the same definition produces byte-identical output that behaves identically.
46	- **Legibility.** The user owns this code. `services.AddRecord<Expense>()` in a generated
47	  registration file is greppable; a controller conjured by a feature provider is not, and the first
48	  time somebody wants to add an endpoint of their own they have to understand the conjuring first.
49	- **Failure mode.** A mis-registration surfaces as a missing route at runtime rather than as a
50	  compile error.
51	
52	So `Cordango.Standalone` keeps the generic controller and the generic store, and the generator emits
53	**explicit registration** for them. The `[Api]` attribute, the assembly scanner, the feature provider
54	and the route convention have no counterpart here.
55	
56	## Piece by piece
57	
58	| Piece | Verdict | Note |
59	|---|---|---|
60	| `IObjectBase<TId>` | **pattern** | Becomes `IRecord`, non-generic: Cordango record ids are `text`. One type parameter fewer everywhere. |
61	| `IHasTrackingFields` | **pattern** | Kept, near-verbatim in shape (`Created`/`CreatedBy`/`LastModified`/`LastModifiedBy`). Set centrally — see the defect below. |
62	| `IHasQueryFields` (`IIsQueryable`) | **dropped** | It declares queryable fields as a `string[]` on the entity. Ours are in the definition already, and the generator emits the filter surface from it. |
63	| `ISoftDelete`, `SoftDeletable` | **dropped for v1** | No Cordango definition expresses soft delete. Adding the interface without the language to reach it is scaffolding for a feature nobody can request. |
64	| `IHasTenantId` | **dropped, by product boundary** | Standalone builds one application for one organisation. Multi-tenancy is the platform. |
65	| `[Api]` attribute, `ApiMethodsToGenerate` | **dropped** | Configuration for runtime discovery. We generate the registration and the method set directly. |
66	| `GenericDbContext` + `ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly` | **pattern, and the best idea here** | `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` per entity is exactly the seam we want: EF's own extension point, one generated file per entity, no reflection needed once we call it explicitly. |
67	| `GenericRepository<T,TId>` | **pattern** | The shape is right, the implementation is not (below). |
68	| Lifecycle hooks `IBeforeCreate<T>` … | **pattern, relocated** | The idea is essential — it is where computed recompute, validation and command-owned-field enforcement live at S7/S8. But see "hooks belong in the container". |
69	| `GenericController<T,TId>` | **pattern** | Route and verb shape carry over. Error handling, permission enforcement and status codes are ours. |
70	| Feature provider, route convention, application part | **dropped** | See above. |
71	| `ApplicationDataService` | **dropped** | A holder for two `DbContext`s and an `HttpContext`. Injecting the `DbContext` directly is clearer and testable with no HTTP context in sight. |
72	| `ExceptionMiddleware` | **pattern** | One place turning an exception into a JSON body is right. Ours emits the Cordango `{code, error}` wire rather than `ValidationProblemDetails`, and does not put `ex.Message` on it. |
73	| Scope-based authorization (`ApiAuthAttribute`, `ValidateScopes`) | **dropped** | Ours is definition-driven: roles, entity grants, per-field overrides, command grants. Not expressible as static scope strings on a type. |
74	| `EFCore.AutomaticMigrations` | **rejected, deliberately** | See below. |
75	| OData, GraphQL, RabbitMQ, Redis, DbFirst | **out of scope** | |
76	
77	## Hooks belong in the container, not on the entity
78	
79	In `TCDev.APIGenerator` a hook is an interface **the POCO itself implements**, and the sample puts
80	business logic in the entity class:
81	
82	```csharp
83	public class Student : IObjectBase<int>, IBeforeCreate<Student>
84	{
85	    public Task<Student> BeforeCreate(Student newItem, IApplicationDataService<...> data) { ... }
86	}
87	```
88	
89	For a hand-written application that is a reasonable convenience. For a **generated** one it is a
90	trap: the entity file is the file the generator overwrites on every build, so the one place the
91	framework invites you to put your logic is the one place that cannot survive a rebuild.
92	
93	`Cordango.Standalone` therefore resolves hooks from the service container:
94	
95	```csharp
96	public interface IBeforeCreate<T> { Task BeforeCreateAsync(T record, RecordContext context, CancellationToken ct); }
97	```
98	
99	Generated hooks land in their own files and register themselves; a hand-written hook is another
100	registration next to them, and both run. The entity stays a POCO — pure data, safe to regenerate —
101	and a hook can be unit-tested with no entity graph and no HTTP context.
102	
103	## Migrations: EF-native, not automatic
104	
105	The sample application calls `app.UseAutomaticApiMigrations()`, which uses `EFCore.AutomaticMigrations`
106	to diff the model against the live database at every startup. The implementation hard-codes
107	`AutomaticMigrationDataLossAllowed = true` on its first call regardless of the `allowDataLoss`
108	argument it was given, and swallows the resulting exception to `Console.WriteLine`.
109	
110	We do the opposite, and it is a decision rather than a preference. The generator invokes EF's own
111	`MigrationsScaffolder` with a pinned migration id, so the migration is a **file in the user's
112	repository that they can read, edit and review in a pull request**; startup runs `Database.Migrate()`.
113	After generation the application evolves by `dotnet ef migrations add` like any other EF project —
114	which is the whole promise of the standalone target: an ordinary application, not one that only our
115	toolchain understands.
116	
117	## Defects found, and what they change
118	
119	Recorded because a generator amplifies: a bug lifted from here would ship in every application
120	Cordango ever emits.
121	
122	**The `IsAssignableFrom` inversion.** Six sites test `typeof(TEntity).IsAssignableFrom(typeof(IHasTrackingFields))`
123	where they mean `IsAssignableTo` — the operands are the wrong way round, so the condition is false
124	for every entity. The consequences are silent: **tracking fields are never populated**, and in
125	`GenericRepository.Delete` the soft-delete branch is never taken, so an entity that opts into
126	`ISoftDelete` is **hard-deleted instead**. The same inversion in `GenericDbContext.OnModelCreating`
127	means the tenant query filter is never applied, which in a multi-tenant deployment is a
128	data-exposure bug rather than a missing feature.
129	
130	The lesson we take: a hand-written type-relationship test, in a place with no test covering the
131	negative case, is worth eliminating rather than getting right. `Cordango.Standalone` sets tracking
132	fields in **one** place — `SaveChanges`, over `ChangeTracker.Entries<IHasTrackingFields>()` — where
133	the compiler enforces the relationship and the wrong direction does not compile.
134	
135	**`async void`.** `GenericRepository.Create` and `.Update` are `async void`. The controller's
136	`repository.Create(record, data); await repository.SaveAsync();` therefore does not await the create
137	— the `BeforeCreate` hook races the save, and any exception the hook throws is unobservable and
138	terminates the process rather than returning a 400. Our equivalents return `Task` and are awaited.
139	
140	**`Update` assigns a local.** `oldRecord = newRecord;` after `Attach(oldRecord)` writes a parameter,
141	not the tracked entity; the line has no effect. The controller separately does
142	`ChangeTracker.Clear(); Update(record)`, which is what actually persists — and which also means the
143	`BeforeUpdate` hook's changes to the old record are discarded, and a client that omits a field
144	writes `null` over it.
145	
146	**`IAfterCreate` calls `BeforeCreate`.** The after-create branch casts to `IBeforeCreate<TEntity>`
147	and invokes `BeforeCreate` a second time.
148	
149	**`Find` dereferences `cacheOptions` unconditionally.** `string.Format(cacheOptions.cacheKey, id)`

# What the standalone scaffold takes from TCDev.APIGenerator

Cordango's standalone target generates a conventional ASP.NET Core application. The question this
document answers, once, is how much of that application should be *generated per entity* and how
much should be *written once and shared* — and whether an existing answer to that question could be
adopted rather than rewritten.

The existing answer assessed here is [DeeJayTC/net-dynamic-api][repo] (`TCDev.APIGenerator`), read at
commit `4279e35`, February 2023, .NET 6. It solves a neighbouring problem: turn annotated POCOs into
a REST API at runtime. Verdicts below are **adopt** (take the package as a dependency), **absorb**
(lift the code), or **pattern** (take the idea, write our own).

[repo]: https://github.com/DeeJayTC/net-dynamic-api

## The verdict in one line

**Pattern, throughout. Nothing is adopted as a dependency and nothing is lifted verbatim.** The
shape of the thing — generic machinery once, thin types per entity — is exactly right and is the
architecture of `Cordango.Standalone`. The mechanism underneath it is built for a problem we do not
have, and the code carries defects a generator would replicate into every application it produced.

## Why not adopt the package

The library targets .NET 6 and its last release is `0.7.1-rc1`. It pulls in Swashbuckle,
Newtonsoft.Json, EntityFramework.Triggers and `EFCore.AutomaticMigrations` transitively, and its
optional modules add OData, GraphQL and RabbitMQ. A generated Cordango application should have a
dependency list its owner can read in one screen and audit themselves; inheriting a stack to get one
generic controller inverts that.

The deeper reason is the one below.

## The mechanism we do not need

`TCDev.APIGenerator` discovers its entities **at runtime, by reflection**: `AddAssembly` scans for
`[Api]`, `GenericTypeControllerFeatureProvider` closes `GenericController<T,TId>` over each
discovered type, `GenericControllerRouteConvention` rewrites the route from the attribute, and
`GenericDbContext.OnModelCreating` calls `ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly` plus `builder.Entity(t)`
for whatever else it found.

That machinery exists to answer a question at startup that **we answer at generation time**. We know
every entity, every route and every key type when we emit the code. Reflection buys us nothing there
and costs three things that matter for a generated artifact:

- **Determinism.** Registration order becomes assembly-scan order. The whole build contract is that
  the same definition produces byte-identical output that behaves identically.
- **Legibility.** The user owns this code. `services.AddRecord<Expense>()` in a generated
  registration file is greppable; a controller conjured by a feature provider is not, and the first
  time somebody wants to add an endpoint of their own they have to understand the conjuring first.
- **Failure mode.** A mis-registration surfaces as a missing route at runtime rather than as a
  compile error.

So `Cordango.Standalone` keeps the generic controller and the generic store, and the generator emits
**explicit registration** for them. The `[Api]` attribute, the assembly scanner, the feature provider
and the route convention have no counterpart here.

## Piece by piece

| Piece | Verdict | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `IObjectBase<TId>` | **pattern** | Becomes `IRecord`, non-generic: Cordango record ids are `text`. One type parameter fewer everywhere. |
| `IHasTrackingFields` | **pattern** | Kept, near-verbatim in shape (`Created`/`CreatedBy`/`LastModified`/`LastModifiedBy`). Set centrally — see the defect below. |
| `IHasQueryFields` (`IIsQueryable`) | **dropped** | It declares queryable fields as a `string[]` on the entity. Ours are in the definition already, and the generator emits the filter surface from it. |
| `ISoftDelete`, `SoftDeletable` | **dropped for v1** | No Cordango definition expresses soft delete. Adding the interface without the language to reach it is scaffolding for a feature nobody can request. |
| `IHasTenantId` | **dropped, by product boundary** | Standalone builds one application for one organisation. Multi-tenancy is the platform. |
| `[Api]` attribute, `ApiMethodsToGenerate` | **dropped** | Configuration for runtime discovery. We generate the registration and the method set directly. |
| `GenericDbContext` + `ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly` | **pattern, and the best idea here** | `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` per entity is exactly the seam we want: EF's own extension point, one generated file per entity, no reflection needed once we call it explicitly. |
| `GenericRepository<T,TId>` | **pattern** | The shape is right, the implementation is not (below). |
| Lifecycle hooks `IBeforeCreate<T>` … | **pattern, relocated** | The idea is essential — it is where computed recompute, validation and command-owned-field enforcement live at S7/S8. But see "hooks belong in the container". |
| `GenericController<T,TId>` | **pattern** | Route and verb shape carry over. Error handling, permission enforcement and status codes are ours. |
| Feature provider, route convention, application part | **dropped** | See above. |
| `ApplicationDataService` | **dropped** | A holder for two `DbContext`s and an `HttpContext`. Injecting the `DbContext` directly is clearer and testable with no HTTP context in sight. |
| `ExceptionMiddleware` | **pattern** | One place turning an exception into a JSON body is right. Ours emits the Cordango `{code, error}` wire rather than `ValidationProblemDetails`, and does not put `ex.Message` on it. |
| Scope-based authorization (`ApiAuthAttribute`, `ValidateScopes`) | **dropped** | Ours is definition-driven: roles, entity grants, per-field overrides, command grants. Not expressible as static scope strings on a type. |
| `EFCore.AutomaticMigrations` | **rejected, deliberately** | See below. |
| OData, GraphQL, RabbitMQ, Redis, DbFirst | **out of scope** | |

## Hooks belong in the container, not on the entity

In `TCDev.APIGenerator` a hook is an interface **the POCO itself implements**, and the sample puts
business logic in the entity class:

```csharp
public class Student : IObjectBase<int>, IBeforeCreate<Student>
{
    public Task<Student> BeforeCreate(Student newItem, IApplicationDataService<...> data) { ... }
}
```

For a hand-written application that is a reasonable convenience. For a **generated** one it is a
trap: the entity file is the file the generator overwrites on every build, so the one place the
framework invites you to put your logic is the one place that cannot survive a rebuild.

`Cordango.Standalone` therefore resolves hooks from the service container:

```csharp
public interface IBeforeCreate<T> { Task BeforeCreateAsync(T record, RecordContext context, CancellationToken ct); }
```

Generated hooks land in their own files and register themselves; a hand-written hook is another
registration next to them, and both run. The entity stays a POCO — pure data, safe to regenerate —
and a hook can be unit-tested with no entity graph and no HTTP context.

## Migrations: EF-native, not automatic

The sample application calls `app.UseAutomaticApiMigrations()`, which uses `EFCore.AutomaticMigrations`
to diff the model against the live database at every startup. The implementation hard-codes
`AutomaticMigrationDataLossAllowed = true` on its first call regardless of the `allowDataLoss`
argument it was given, and swallows the resulting exception to `Console.WriteLine`.

We do the opposite, and it is a decision rather than a preference. The generator invokes EF's own
`MigrationsScaffolder` with a pinned migration id, so the migration is a **file in the user's
repository that they can read, edit and review in a pull request**; startup runs `Database.Migrate()`.
After generation the application evolves by `dotnet ef migrations add` like any other EF project —
which is the whole promise of the standalone target: an ordinary application, not one that only our
toolchain understands.

## Defects found, and what they change

Recorded because a generator amplifies: a bug lifted from here would ship in every application
Cordango ever emits.

**The `IsAssignableFrom` inversion.** Six sites test `typeof(TEntity).IsAssignableFrom(typeof(IHasTrackingFields))`
where they mean `IsAssignableTo` — the operands are the wrong way round, so the condition is false
for every entity. The consequences are silent: **tracking fields are never populated**, and in
`GenericRepository.Delete` the soft-delete branch is never taken, so an entity that opts into
`ISoftDelete` is **hard-deleted instead**. The same inversion in `GenericDbContext.OnModelCreating`
means the tenant query filter is never applied, which in a multi-tenant deployment is a
data-exposure bug rather than a missing feature.

The lesson we take: a hand-written type-relationship test, in a place with no test covering the
negative case, is worth eliminating rather than getting right. `Cordango.Standalone` sets tracking
fields in **one** place — `SaveChanges`, over `ChangeTracker.Entries<IHasTrackingFields>()` — where
the compiler enforces the relationship and the wrong direction does not compile.

**`async void`.** `GenericRepository.Create` and `.Update` are `async void`. The controller's
`repository.Create(record, data); await repository.SaveAsync();` therefore does not await the create
— the `BeforeCreate` hook races the save, and any exception the hook throws is unobservable and
terminates the process rather than returning a 400. Our equivalents return `Task` and are awaited.

**`Update` assigns a local.** `oldRecord = newRecord;` after `Attach(oldRecord)` writes a parameter,
not the tracked entity; the line has no effect. The controller separately does
`ChangeTracker.Clear(); Update(record)`, which is what actually persists — and which also means the
`BeforeUpdate` hook's changes to the old record are discarded, and a client that omits a field
writes `null` over it.

**`IAfterCreate` calls `BeforeCreate`.** The after-create branch casts to `IBeforeCreate<TEntity>`
and invokes `BeforeCreate` a second time.

**`Find` dereferences `cacheOptions` unconditionally.** `string.Format(cacheOptions.cacheKey, id)`
runs whenever an `ICacheService` is registered, but `cacheOptions` is only non-null when the entity
carries `[Cachable]` — a `NullReferenceException` for every uncached entity in a Redis-enabled app.

**`Get(id)` compares `e.Id.ToString() == id.ToString()`.** Either it fails to translate to SQL and
loads the table, or it translates to a cast that cannot use the primary key index.

**Exception detail on the wire.** Both the controller (`return BadRequest(ex.Message)`) and
`ExceptionMiddleware` (`Detail = ex.Message`) hand raw exception text to the caller. Ours maps to a
stable `{code, error}` pair and logs the exception server-side.

**The Postgres provider does not use Postgres.** `TCDev.APIGenerator.Data.Postgres`'s
`ProviderConfig.OnConfiguring` calls `optionsBuilder.UseSqlServer(...)`, and its `AddDataContextSQL`
extension is `private`, so it is unreachable from outside the assembly. The `src/Data/**` tree looks
like a half-finished restructure of `src/TCDev.APIGenerator.*`; both copies are in the solution.

## What this leaves us

The architecture is Tim's, and it survives the assessment intact:

> generic machinery written once and compiled into a library; thin, regenerable, per-entity types;
> `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` as the mapping seam; lifecycle hooks as the extension point;
> EF migrations as the schema story.

What changes is that **registration is generated rather than discovered**, **hooks live in the
container rather than on the entity**, **tracking fields are set once where the type system can check
it**, and **migrations are files the user owns**. Those four are the difference between a runtime
framework and a code generator, which is the difference between the two projects.

content.text: I've mapped the architecture first-hand. The good news: the seam you're asking about already exists and was designed for exactly this. Let me confirm a few product decisions while my exploration agents finish.

questions.question: Which Node stack should the generated backend be?

options.label: TypeScript + Fastify + Prisma (Recommended)
options.description: Closest fit to the repo's stated doctrine: explicit route registration (no decorator conjuring), Prisma migrations land as SQL files the owner reads and reviews (mirrors the EF 'migrations are files you own' decision), and a dependency list that fits on one screen.
options.preview:
api/
  src/
    server.ts          explicit route registration
    records/            generic store, one module per entity
    entities/expense.ts thin, regenerable
    hooks/              container-resolved, hand-written ones sit beside
  prisma/
    schema.prisma
    migrations/0001_init/migration.sql   <- reviewable in a PR

options.label: TypeScript + NestJS + TypeORM
options.description: Structurally the nearest mirror of ASP.NET Core: DI container, controllers, guards, modules. The shape transfers almost 1:1, only syntax changes. Costs a large dependency tree and the decorator/discovery magic the APIGenerator assessment argued against.
options.preview:
api/src/
  app.module.ts
  expense/
    expense.controller.ts   @Controller('api/expense')
    expense.entity.ts       @Entity()
    expense.module.ts
  common/guards/permissions.guard.ts

// mirrors C# 1:1, but registration is discovered, not generated

options.label: TypeScript + Express + Drizzle
options.description: Lightest option. Drizzle is TypeScript-native and generates SQL migration files too. Express is the most familiar to the widest audience but the least structured of the three.
options.preview:
api/src/
  server.ts
  routes/expense.ts
  db/schema.ts        drizzle table defs
  drizzle/0000_init.sql

// smallest surface, least opinionated

questions.question: Should the Node target emit the SAME Vue frontend the .NET target emits?

options.label: Same Vue, shared emitter (Recommended)
options.description: node-vue reuses the identical WebEmitter and web/ template tree. Changes exactly ONE axis, so any difference in the running app is provably the backend. Forces the HTTP wire contract to be written down, which is the thing that makes any future frontend swappable.
options.preview:
dotnet-vue  =  DotNetBackend  +  VueFrontend
node-vue    =  NodeBackend    +  VueFrontend
                    ^^^^                ^^^^
              only this changes   byte-identical

They meet at one written contract:
  GET/POST/PUT/DELETE /api/{entity}
  { items, total } | { code, error, fields }
  cookie session + XSRF-TOKEN header
  /api/media, /api/directory/person

options.label: Node target brings its own frontend copy
options.description: No refactor needed up front; the Node generator carries a duplicate of the Vue emitter and templates. Fastest to first output, but the two copies start drifting on day one and there is no contract keeping them honest.

options.label: Go straight to node-react
options.description: Change both axes at once for the most striking demo. Most work, and when the generated app misbehaves you cannot tell whether the backend or the frontend is at fault.
options.preview:
dotnet-vue  =  DotNetBackend + VueFrontend
node-react  =  NodeBackend   + ReactFrontend
                    ^^^^           ^^^^
              both change at once

// impressive, but no controlled comparison

questions.question: How much of the .NET target's behaviour must the first Node target reach?

options.label: Runs the app; gaps are LOUD (Recommended)
options.description: Data model, migrations, REST, permissions, sign-in, seed, and the Vue frontend boots and does real CRUD against it. Workflows, commands, computed fields report as CORD23xx 'not generated yet' and need --allow-incomplete. This is exactly how dotnet-vue itself was built.
options.preview:
S-N1  entities + prisma schema + migration
S-N2  generic store + REST + permissions
S-N3  sign-in, media, directory
S-N4  seed + docker compose up
      -> same Vue app, real CRUD

Not yet:  workflows, commands, computed
          reported, never silently dropped

options.label: Full parity with dotnet-vue
options.description: Every emitter reaches the same bar before the target ships: workflows, command guards, effects, computed recompute cascade. Much larger, and the recompute cascade is the hardest piece in the whole product.

questions.question: Should the Node generator be a C# project that emits TypeScript, or a separate Node program speaking a stdin/stdout protocol?

options.label: In-process C# generator (Recommended)
options.description: A new Cordango.SourceGen.NodeVue project implementing IAppSourceGenerator, emitting TypeScript. Reuses AppModel, TargetValidator, capabilities and the whole test suite. Your stated goal is a target LANGUAGE, and this delivers it fully.
options.preview:
src/Cordango.SourceGen.NodeVue/
  NodeVueGenerator.cs  : IAppSourceGenerator
  Emit/PrismaEmitter.cs
  Emit/RouteEmitter.cs

Targets.cs:
  [new DotNetVueGenerator(), new NodeVueGenerator()]

// cordango build --target node-vue

options.label: Out-of-process protocol
options.description: A Node program receiving the compiled artifact on stdin and returning files on stdout, per the protocol Contracts.cs already anticipates. Proves third parties can write targets in their own language, but adds protocol, discovery, versioning and packaging work before a single line is emitted.

### Verdict on separation
**Separated by class, not by folder or namespace.** `WebEmitter` is the sole frontend emitter and every other emitter is backend — a clean 1:N split. But all 11 emitters sit in one `Emit/` directory under one namespace `Cordango.SourceGen.DotNetVue.Emit`, and they share:
- `Emit\Source.cs` — the text builder (`Line`/`Open`/`Close`/`Indent`; C#-brace-flavoured but used for Vue too with `new Source(2)`)
- `Model\Naming.cs` — `Pascal` :22, `Camel` :46, `Type` :80, `Property` :145, `Table` :153, `Column` :157, `Sanitise` :162, `Literal` :177 (C#), `JsLiteral` :201 (JS)
- `Model\AppModel.cs` — consumed by both halves

So there is no `Backend/` vs `Web/` folder boundary and no interface either half implements. The seam a second *language* target would fork along is the emitter set as a whole, not backend-vs-frontend.

## How a second language target plugs in

**Required changes (small):**
1. New project referencing `Cordango.SourceGen`; implement `IAppSourceGenerator`.
2. Add an instance to `Targets.Registered` — `src\Cordango.Cli\Generate\Targets.cs:24`; optionally an alias at `:35`.
3. Add a `ProjectReference` in `src\Cordango.Cli\Cordango.Cli.csproj` (the three refs at :~110).
4. Declare `GeneratorCapabilities`; embed your own scaffold with the same `EmbeddedResource`/`LogicalName` pattern.

**Nothing above `Targets.cs` needs touching** — `BuildCommand`, `CheckCommand`, `TargetsCommand`, `TargetValidator`, `GeneratedFileWriter`, `BuildMetadata` are all target-agnostic already.

**Frictions a second target will hit:**
- **`AppModel` is in the wrong project.** It is the natural IR for any target but ~40 % of it is .NET-specific (`ClrType`, `DeclaredType`, `IsValueType`, `Initialiser`, `TypeName`, `Namespace`, `Table`, `Column`). A second target either duplicates it or it gets split into a neutral core (promoted to `Cordango.SourceGen`) plus per-target naming/typing. Same question for `Source` and `Naming`.
- **`ComputedEmitter` / `ConditionEmitter` encode language semantics** (null discipline, unknown-propagation on divide/min/max/pow — see `ComputedEmitter.cs:9-37`). Those rules are the language's, not .NET's, and a second target must re-derive them. Highest-risk duplication in the repo, by the file's own admission ("the platform and a generated application computing different totals from one definition is the worst failure this project has").
- **`CapabilityCoverageTests` hardcodes the target** — `tests\Compatibility.Tests\CapabilityCoverageTests.cs:25` (`new DotNetVueGenerator().Capabilities`). Same in `StandaloneCompatibilityTests.cs:35`. Both need to become theories over `Targets.All`.
- **CORD23xx codes are magic strings**, not in `DiagnosticCodes.cs`: `CORD2301` (`WebEmitter.cs:310`), `CORD2302/2303/2305/2306` (`DotNetVueGenerator.cs:272, 296, 314, 332, 283, 324`). A second target inventing its own numbering will collide.
- **The "declared capability vs actually emitted" split** is per-target ad hoc: `WorkflowEmitter.Emitted` :28 / `.Triggers` :34 shadow the declared `Capabilities`, reconciled by hand in `DotNetVueGenerator.NotYetEmitted` :257. There is no SDK concept for it.
- **The out-of-process (stdin/stdout) protocol has zero implementation.** It is described in three doc comments only — `Contracts.cs:98-99`, `GeneratorCapabilities.cs:55-56`, `Targets.cs:19-20`. Confirmed by grep.
- `Cordango.SourceGen` is **deliberately unpublished** (csproj comment, "NOT PUBLISHED YET"): the stated reason is that an interface designed against one implementation fits it and fights the next. A second target is precisely the event that should freeze it.
- Minor: `DotNetVueGenerator` reads options via `request.Options?["x"]?.GetValue<bool>()` (:157-158, :213) instead of the `GenerateRequest.Flag`/`Option` accessors (`Contracts.cs:48-52`) — worth normalizing before a second consumer copies the pattern.

**Prior-art context:** `docs\apigenerator-assessment.md` (177 lines) records the architectural stance for the DotNet target — generic machinery in a library, thin regenerable per-entity types, `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` as the mapping seam, hooks in the DI container (never on the entity, because the entity file is overwritten), migrations as user-owned files, **registration generated rather than discovered**. Those four principles are the ones a second target should mirror in its own idiom.</result>
