=== conditions README ===
# Condition decision fixtures

These files are the contract between two implementations of one small language.

A `when` in the definition — on a command, on a workflow, on a rollup's filters — is the same shape
everywhere: nested `all` / `any` over leaves of `{ field, operator, value }`. Cordango Platform
evaluates it in `Cordango.Semantics.ConditionEvaluator`. A standalone application generated by this
toolchain evaluates it with *different* code, in `Cordango.Standalone.Conditions.ConditionEvaluator`.

The duplication is deliberate, for the same reason the [permission fixtures](../permissions/) exist:
sharing the implementation would mean a change made for one product's reasons silently altering the
other's behaviour, and "silently" is the problem. A condition decides whether an approval is allowed
and whether a workflow fires. Nobody notices it answering wrongly until a month of records went the
wrong way.

So the rules are pinned here as **data**, and both implementations are asserted against the same data
by their own suites. Two implementations that must agree, and a test that fails the moment they stop.

## What these pin, and why each one is here

1. **`01` — comparison picks its rule from the operands.** A definition writes `value: 10000` as a
   JSON number and `stage: "lead"` as text; a record holds a decimal column and a text column. Both
   have to work without anybody declaring a type. Numbers compare as numbers even when one side is
   written as a string, because `9 > 10` is false and `"9" > "10"` is true.

2. **`02` — a blank is not comparable.** The rule every naive implementation gets wrong. Treating a
   missing number as zero makes `amount lt 100` true for every record nobody has filled in, and a
   workflow built on it fires on untouched rows. `lt` and `gt` are both false against a blank, which
   means they are not each other's negation — that is intended and it is worth knowing.

3. **`03` — the list operators, and the two boundary rules.** `between` is inclusive at both ends.
   `overlaps` depends on whether the endpoints carry a time: a bare DATE names a whole day, so a
   range ending Monday overlaps a window starting Monday, while anything with a time is half-open so
   a meeting ending at 10:00 does not collide with one starting at 10:00. That distinction is the
   entire point of a conflict check, and the front end applies the identical rule.

4. **`04` — composition and the value tokens.** `{{actor.id}}` makes one stored condition answer
   differently for two people. `{{today}}` and its day offsets come from the clock the caller passed,
   never from the machine, so a test can ask what a workflow would have done last March.

5. **`05` — nothing matches by accident.** Shapes that should never reach a running application,
   because the gate rejects them at author time. Pinned anyway: the safe reading of "I do not
   understand this guard" is that the guarded thing does not happen. A leaf naming neither a field
   nor a path is the sharp one — without a rule it would compare null against null and answer *true*.

## Format

```json
{
  "name": "what this file settles",
  "why": "why it is worth pinning",
  "now": "2026-03-15T10:00:00Z",     // the clock, for {{today}}
  "actorId": "person-001",           // who is asking, for {{actor.id}}
  "cases": [
    {
      "why": "optional, per case",
      "record":    { "stage": "lead" },
      "condition": { "field": "stage", "operator": "eq", "value": "lead" },
      "expect": true
    }
  ]
}
```

`record` is the record as JSON, exactly as the database holds it. `condition` is the definition's own
shape. `expect` is the answer both implementations must give.

## Adding one

Add a case whenever a condition surprises you, and write down in `why` what the surprise was. That
sentence is the actual deliverable — the assertion only stops the regression, while the sentence is
what stops somebody "fixing" the behaviour back.

Both suites pick up new files automatically:

- `dotnet test oss/cordango/Cordango.slnx` — the standalone implementation
- `dotnet test backend/AppBuilder.slnx` — the platform implementation

## One thing these do not pin

The generated application does not carry the JSON above. `ConditionEmitter` turns it into C# at build
time — `Condition.Leaf("stage", "eq", "lead")` — and the runtime evaluates *that*. So these fixtures
pin the two evaluators against each other, and the emitter's translation is pinned separately, by its
own tests and by compiling every generated application.

=== conditions dir ===
01-equality-and-types.json
02-blank-is-not-comparable.json
03-lists-ranges-and-text.json
04-composition-and-tokens.json
05-nothing-matches-by-accident.json

content.text:
Confirmed, and it's a real finding. The platform evaluator carefully preserves "cannot say" as null in `Compare`, then **throws it away at the very next boolean operator**:

| expression (a=1, b=0 → `a/b` is unknown) | platform says |
|---|---|
| `(a / b) < 1` | `null` — unknown, correct |
| `not ((a / b) < 1)` | **`True`** — unknown coerced to false, then negated |
| `((a / b) < 1) and true` | **`False`** — unknown coerced to false |
| `((a/b)<1) == ((a/b)<1)` | **`True`** — two unknowns compare equal |

That contradicts the doctrine `Calc.cs` states in its own header ("it stays unknown through everything downstream"). Let me check what the generator emits for the same shapes.

input.command:
mkdir -p tests/fixtures/computed && cat > tests/fixtures/computed/README.md <<'MDEOF'
# Computed expression fixtures

These files are the contract between the implementations of one small arithmetic.

A `computed.expr` in the definition — `total_revenue - total_costs`, `done_tasks * 100 / total_tasks`,
`min(usage, plan.cap)` — has to give the same answer everywhere it is worked out. Cordango Platform
evaluates it with `ComputedExpr.EvaluateValue`. A standalone application does not evaluate it at all:
`ComputedEmitter` turns it into a C# method at build time and the generated code computes it. Same
definition, same figures expected, two entirely different mechanisms.

That is a sharper split than the [condition fixtures](../conditions/) face, and the consequence is
worse. `ComputedEmitter` says so in its own header:

> the platform and a generated application computing different totals from one definition is the
> worst failure this project has.

A guard that answers wrongly sends one approval the wrong way and somebody notices. A total that is
quietly different in two places is found a quarter later by somebody reconciling two reports, and by
then every figure derived from it is wrong too.

So the rules are pinned here as **data**, and each implementation is asserted against the same data by
its own suite.

## The rule underneath all of them

**A blank field is zero. A figure that could not be worked out is unknown. They are not the same.**

A record with no tax has a tax of nothing, and a total that refused to add it up would be blank on
every half-filled row — so a blank NUMBER reads as zero and a blank BOOLEAN reads as false. But a
division by zero, a bound with an unknown side, a power that overflows, a duration missing an
endpoint: none of those is zero and none is an error. They are unknown, and a cap computed from an
unknown bound must not silently become no cap at all.

The distinction is easy to state and easy to lose. `min(a, b)` where both fields are blank is
**zero**, because both read as zero. `min(a, 1 / 0)` is **unknown**, because one side could not be
worked out. Most of what is pinned below is that one sentence, applied.

## What these pin, and why each one is here

1. **`01` — a blank is zero, and unknown is not.** The two kinds of missing, side by side, and what
   each does to the arithmetic around it. A blank is absorbed (`blank + 1` is `1`); an unknown
   spreads (`(1 / 0) + 1` is unknown).

2. **`02` — bounds and powers refuse to guess.** `min` and `max` are how a row states a cap on one of
   its own figures, and returning the other side when one is unknown would silently un-cap it. `pow`
   goes through `double` and comes back through a checked conversion, so overflow and NaN are
   unknown rather than an exception inside a total somebody was only reading.

3. **`03` — a duration needs both ends.** `days_between` on a record whose end date is not set is not
   a very long time and not zero. Fractional for a `datetime`, whole for a `date`.

4. **`04` — a comparison can say "cannot say".** The sharp one. Two blank number fields compare as
   `0 < 0`, which is **false** — a definite answer, because blanks are zeros. But a comparison over
   an unknown is **unknown**, which is neither true nor false. A bare `<` on two nullables in C#
   answers false for both, which would make a rule keyed on "is the balance below the threshold" fire
   on every record whose balance has not been computed yet.

## Format

```json
{
  "name": "what this file settles",
  "why": "why it is worth pinning",
  "fields": {
    "revenue": { "type": "decimal" },
    "months":  { "type": "integer", "required": true },
    "start":   { "type": "datetime" }
  },
  "cases": [
    {
      "why": "optional, per case",
      "record": { "revenue": 100, "months": 4 },
      "expr":   "revenue / months",
      "expect": 25
    }
  ]
}
```

`fields` declares the entity the expression is written against. It is needed and not optional: an
identifier's TYPE decides what its comparisons mean, and whether a field is `required` decides
whether the generated C# reads it as `r.X` or as `(r.X ?? 0m)`.

`record` is the record as the database holds it; a key left out is a field nobody has filled in.
`expr` is the definition's own string. `expect` is the answer every implementation must give — a JSON
number, `true`, `false`, or `null` for unknown.

## Adding one

Add a case whenever a figure surprises you, and write down in `why` what the surprise was. That
sentence is the actual deliverable — the assertion only stops the regression, while the sentence is
what stops somebody "fixing" the behaviour back.

- `dotnet test oss/cordango/Cordango.slnx` — the evaluator, and that the generator writes or refuses
  every shape used here
- `dotnet test backend/AppBuilder.slnx` — the platform implementation

## What these do not yet pin

**That the generated C# gives these answers when it RUNS.** `ComputedFixtureTests` asserts two things:
that the evaluator agrees with the fixture, and that `ComputedEmitter` produces something for every
shape the fixtures use rather than silently refusing it. Neither runs the emitted code.

`GeneratedArithmeticTests` does run it — it builds a real application, loads it and calls the computed
methods — but against expressions that happen to be in a corpus app rather than against these files.
Until those two meet, an expression that emits C# which compiles and returns the wrong number is
caught here only if the evaluator disagrees with the fixture, not if the emitter does.

Nor are the fixtures hand-written from an implementation. They are written from the rules above, which
is the same discipline the [permission fixtures](../permissions/) state and for the same reason:
recording would make one implementation the definition of correct and enshrine its bugs as the
contract the other has to match.
MDEOF

All suites green — 1623 tests, 0 failures. `Corpus.cs` only walks `historical`/`interactive` under fixtures, so the new directory doesn't trip the corpus count tripwires.

While writing these I found three defects in the in-flight S8 computed work, all latent because **no corpus app has a computed field using a comparison or boolean logic** — so the path has never been exercised. I need your call on one of them before I write the fixtures that would pin it.

questions.question: When a computed figure is unknown, what should `and` / `or` / `not` / `==` do with it? The platform and the generator currently disagree, and both contradict the doctrine written in Calc.cs.

options.label: Three-valued — unknown propagates (Recommended)
options.description: Honours the rule already written in Calc.cs and ComputedEmitter's headers. The generated side is ALREADY three-valued except for the compile bug: C#'s & and | on bool? are exactly Kleene logic, so this is a two-character fix there. Cost: the platform evaluator changes, which changes behaviour on the hosted product.
options.preview:
a=1, b=0  so  (a/b) is unknown

  (a/b) < 1              -> unknown
  not ((a/b) < 1)        -> unknown
  ((a/b) < 1) and true   -> unknown
  ((a/b) < 1) and false  -> FALSE   <- still definite
  ((a/b) < 1) or  true   -> TRUE    <- still definite

Generated: swap && -> &, || -> |  (bool? & bool? IS Kleene)
           ! and Calc.Same already correct
Platform:  Bool(n) must stop coercing null -> false

options.label: Two-valued — unknown reads as false
options.description: Matches what the platform does today, so nothing on the hosted product changes. The generator gets explicit coercion so it compiles and agrees. Cost: 'cannot say' silently becomes 'no' — the exact failure Calc.Compare's own doc comment says it exists to prevent.

  not ((a/b) < 1)        -> TRUE    <- unknown became false,
  ((a/b) < 1) and true   -> FALSE      then got negated
  ((a/b) < 1) == ((a/b) < 1) -> TRUE

Generated: emit (x ?? false) && (y ?? false)
                !(x ?? false)

Platform:  unchanged

Calc.Compare keeps null... and every caller drops it.

private static ComputedValue Eval(Node node,
        Func<string, decimal?> numberValue,
        Func<string, bool?> booleanValue,
        Func<string, DateTimeOffset?> dateValue,
        Func<string, decimal?>? prevValue = null)
    {
        decimal? Num(Node n) => Eval(n, numberValue, booleanValue, dateValue, prevValue).Number;
        bool Bool(Node n) => Eval(n, numberValue, booleanValue, dateValue, prevValue).Boolean == true;
        DateTimeOffset? Date(Node n) => Eval(n, numberValue, booleanValue, dateValue, prevValue).Date;

        return node switch
        {
                Compare(Date(b.Left), Date(b.Right), (a, c) => a == c),
            BinaryNode { Op: "!=", Left.Kind: ComputedValueKind.Date } b =>
                Compare(Date(b.Left), Date(b.Right), (a, c) => a != c),
            BinaryNode { Op: "==" } b => ComputedValue.FromBoolean(Bool(b.Left) == Bool(b.Right)),
            BinaryNode { Op: "!=" } b => ComputedValue.FromBoolean(Bool(b.Left) != Bool(b.Right)),
            BinaryNode { Op: "and" } b => ComputedValue.FromBoolean(Bool(b.Left) && Bool(b.Right)),
            BinaryNode { Op: "or" } b => ComputedValue.FromBoolean(Bool(b.Left) || Bool(b.Right)),
            FunctionNode { Name: "pow" } f => ComputedValue.FromNumber(Power(Num(f.Left), Num(f.Right))),
            FunctionNode { Name: "min" } f => ComputedValue.FromNumber(Bound(Num(f.Left), Num(f.Right), lower: true)),
            FunctionNode { Name: "max" } f => ComputedValue.FromNumber(Bound(Num(f.Left), Num(f.Right), lower: false)),
            DurationNode d => ComputedValue.FromNumber(Duration(d.Name, dateValue(d.From), dateValue(d.To))),

fixtures.

# Computed expression fixtures

These files are the contract between the implementations of one small arithmetic.

A `computed.expr` in the definition — `total_revenue - total_costs`, `done_tasks * 100 / total_tasks`,
`min(usage, plan.cap)` — has to give the same answer everywhere it is worked out. Cordango Platform
evaluates it with `ComputedExpr.EvaluateValue`. A standalone application does not evaluate it at all:
`ComputedEmitter` turns it into a C# method at build time and the generated code computes it. Same
definition, same figures expected, two entirely different mechanisms.

That is a sharper split than the [condition fixtures](../conditions/) face, and the consequence is
worse. `ComputedEmitter` says so in its own header:

> the platform and a generated application computing different totals from one definition is the
> worst failure this project has.

A guard that answers wrongly sends one approval the wrong way and somebody notices. A total that is
quietly different in two places is found a quarter later by somebody reconciling two reports, and by
then every figure derived from it is wrong too.

So the rules are pinned here as **data**, and each implementation is asserted against the same data by
its own suite.

## The rule underneath all of them

**A blank field is zero. A figure that could not be worked out is unknown. They are not the same.**

A record with no tax has a tax of nothing, and a total that refused to add it up would be blank on
every half-filled row — so a blank NUMBER reads as zero and a blank BOOLEAN reads as false. But a
division by zero, a bound with an unknown side, a power that overflows, a duration missing an
endpoint: none of those is zero and none is an error. They are unknown, and a cap computed from an
unknown bound must not silently become no cap at all.

The distinction is easy to state and easy to lose. `min(a, b)` where both fields are blank is
**zero**, because both read as zero. `min(a, 1 / 0)` is **unknown**, because one side could not be
worked out. Most of what is pinned below is that one sentence, applied.

## What these pin, and why each one is here

1. **`01` — a blank is zero, and unknown is not.** The two kinds of missing, side by side, and what
   each does to the arithmetic around it. A blank is absorbed (`blank + 1` is `1`); an unknown
   spreads (`(1 / 0) + 1` is unknown).

2. **`02` — bounds and powers refuse to guess.** `min` and `max` are how a row states a cap on one of
   its own figures, and returning the other side when one is unknown would silently un-cap it. `pow`
   goes through `double` and comes back through a checked conversion, so overflow and NaN are
   unknown rather than an exception inside a total somebody was only reading.

3. **`03` — a duration needs both ends.** `days_between` on a record whose end date is not set is not
   a very long time and not zero. Fractional for a `datetime`, whole for a `date`.

4. **`04` — a comparison can say "cannot say".** The sharp one. Two blank number fields compare as
   `0 < 0`, which is **false** — a definite answer, because blanks are zeros. But a comparison over
   an unknown is **unknown**, which is neither true nor false. A bare `<` on two nullables in C#
   answers false for both, which would make a rule keyed on "is the balance below the threshold" fire
   on every record whose balance has not been computed yet.

## Format

```json
{
  "name": "what this file settles",
  "why": "why it is worth pinning",
  "fields": {
    "revenue": { "type": "decimal" },
    "months":  { "type": "integer", "required": true },
    "start":   { "type": "datetime" }
  },
  "cases": [
    {
      "why": "optional, per case",
      "record": { "revenue": 100, "months": 4 },
      "expr":   "revenue / months",
      "expect": 25
    }
  ]
}
```

`fields` declares the entity the expression is written against. It is needed and not optional: an
identifier's TYPE decides what its comparisons mean, and whether a field is `required` decides
whether the generated C# reads it as `r.X` or as `(r.X ?? 0m)`.

`record` is the record as the database holds it; a key left out is a field nobody has filled in.
`expr` is the definition's own string. `expect` is the answer every implementation must give — a JSON
number, `true`, `false`, or `null` for unknown.

## Adding one

Add a case whenever a figure surprises you, and write down in `why` what the surprise was. That
sentence is the actual deliverable — the assertion only stops the regression, while the sentence is
what stops somebody "fixing" the behaviour back.

- `dotnet test oss/cordango/Cordango.slnx` — the evaluator, and that the generator writes or refuses
  every shape used here
- `dotnet test backend/AppBuilder.slnx` — the platform implementation

## What these do not yet pin

**That the generated C# gives these answers when it RUNS.** `ComputedFixtureTests` asserts two things:
that the evaluator agrees with the fixture, and that `ComputedEmitter` produces something for every
shape the fixtures use rather than silently refusing it. Neither runs the emitted code.

`GeneratedArithmeticTests` does run it — it builds a real application, loads it and calls the computed
methods — but against expressions that happen to be in a corpus app rather than against these files.
Until those two meet, an expression that emits C# which compiles and returns the wrong number is
caught here only if the evaluator disagrees with the fixture, not if the emitter does.

Nor are the fixtures hand-written from an implementation. They are written from the rules above, which
is the same discipline the [permission fixtures](../permissions/) state and for the same reason:
recording would make one implementation the definition of correct and enshrine its bugs as the
contract the other has to match.

## Phase 0 — Finish S8 on `dotnet-vue` (prerequisite)

Mostly not this plan's work; named because it gates Phase 1. Existing plan:
`~/.claude/plans/heres-a-pretty-extensive-glimmering-lobster.md:319-324`.

### ✅ DONE — `tests/fixtures/computed/` (the one addition this plan depended on)

Five hand-written files, 57 cases, plus `tests/Standalone.Tests/ComputedFixtureTests.cs`
(evaluator + write-or-refuse + guard-the-guard). Written from the documented rules, never recorded
from an implementation, per `tests/fixtures/permissions/README.md:57-59`.

Writing them surfaced three defects in the in-flight S8 work, all latent because **no corpus app has
a computed field using a comparison or boolean logic** — the path had never been exercised:

1. **`and` / `or` over a comparison did not compile.** `((a/b) < 1) and true` emitted
   `(Calc.Compare(…) && true)`, and `&&` is not defined on `bool?` — CS0019, whole application fails
   to build. **Fixed**: `&&`→`&`, `||`→`|` in `ComputedEmitter.Binary`.
2. **`not` over a comparison diverged** — generated gave unknown, platform gave `true`.
3. **`==` over two unknown comparisons diverged** — generated gave unknown, platform gave `true`.

Under 2 and 3 was a real semantic hole: `ComputedExpr.Eval`'s `Bool()` coerced unknown→false, so
`Compare` carefully answered null and the very next boolean operator threw it away — contradicting
the doctrine written in `Calc.cs`'s own header. **Tim's decision: three-valued (Kleene) logic,
unknown propagates.** Applied to `ComputedExpr.Eval` (`Truth()` returns `bool?`; `&`/`|` on `bool?`
are already Kleene; `SameTruth`/`DifferentTruth` because C#'s lifted `==` is two-valued in disguise).

One thing this changed on the hosted product: the platform runtime calls `ComputedExpr` directly

---
name: computed-unknown-is-three-valued
description: Computed expressions use Kleene three-valued logic — unknown propagates through and/or/not/==; decided 2026-08-22 and applied to the ONE shared evaluator
metadata:
  type: project
---

Decided 2026-08-22 while writing `tests/fixtures/computed/`: **a computed figure that could not be
worked out stays unknown through `and`, `or`, `not` and `==`.** Three-valued (Kleene) logic, not
"unknown reads as false".

A blank FIELD is still zero (number) or false (boolean) — that never changed. What propagates is the
*other* kind of missing: divide by zero, a bound with an unknown side, an overflowing `pow`, a
duration missing an endpoint.

**Why:** `Compare` had always answered null for a comparison it could not make, and then
`ComputedExpr.Eval`'s `Bool()` coerced that straight back to false at the very next operator. So
`not ((a / b) < 1)` on a blank divisor answered **true** — the evaluator quietly deciding a figure
nobody could work out was below the threshold. That contradicted the doctrine already written in
`Calc.cs`'s own header ("it stays unknown through everything downstream").

Kleene keeps the answers that are still definite: `unknown AND false` is false, `unknown OR true` is
true. Only where the unknown could change the answer does the answer go unknown.

**How to apply:**
- There is **ONE** evaluator, not two. `ComputedExpr` lives in `Cordango.Compiler` and the platform
  runtime calls it directly — so changing it changes the hosted product. This is a real difference
  from [[cord-oss-cli]]'s permission and condition fixtures, which pin two independent
  implementations against each other. For computed, the second implementation is the **emitted C#**.
- In C#, `&` and `|` on `bool?` ARE Kleene; `&&` and `||` are **not defined on `bool?` at all**
  (CS0019). `!` on `bool?` is already correct. But `==` on two `bool?` is C#'s lifted equality, which
  is two-valued in disguise (`null == null` → true) — write it out explicitly.
- Finding this needed a fixture, because **no corpus app has a computed field using a comparison or
  boolean logic**. Three defects sat latent behind that, including one that made the whole generated
  application fail to build. When adding a language feature, check whether any corpus app actually
  exercises it before trusting a green suite.

Related: [[computed-expr-min-max]] (the same null-in/null-out discipline for bounds),
[[calculation-plane]], [[cord-oss-cli]].

content.text:
Done. Here's where things stand.

## The architecture answer

**A target stays one whole stack; split the code, not the target.** `IAppSourceGenerator` already means "one target stack", and [Targets.cs](oss/cordango/src/Cordango.Cli/Generate/Targets.cs) was built for a second one. Sharing happens by promoting neutral code into the SDK — `AppModel` (~60% neutral), `Source.cs` (already width-parameterised for C# and JS), and `WebEmitter` + the 39 web templates into a `Cordango.Web.Vue` both targets embed. `node-react` later is N+M, not N×M, but that abstraction waits until two real targets show where the seam falls.

Full plan approved and saved, now updated with what landed.

## What I built

Phase 1 collides with your in-flight S8 edits, so I started where the plan said it was safe and the value was highest: **`tests/fixtures/computed/`** — 5 hand-written files, 57 cases, plus [ComputedFixtureTests.cs](oss/cordango/tests/Standalone.Tests/ComputedFixtureTests.cs).

Writing them found **three defects in the S8 computed work**, all latent because no corpus app has a computed field using a comparison or boolean logic:

1. **`and`/`or` over a comparison didn't compile.** `((a/b) < 1) and true` emitted `(Calc.Compare(…) && true)` — `&&` isn't defined on `bool?`. CS0019, whole application fails to build. Fixed: `&&`→`&`, `||`→`|`.
2. **`not` over a comparison diverged** — generated gave unknown, platform gave `true`.
3. **`==` over two unknown comparisons diverged** — same split.

Under 2 and 3 sat the real hole you decided on: `Compare` answered null carefully and the next boolean operator threw it away. Three-valued logic now applied to `ComputedExpr.Eval`.

## Two things worth knowing

**There is only ONE computed evaluator, not two.** The platform runtime calls `ComputedExpr` directly rather than carrying its own copy — unlike permissions and conditions. So this change *is* a hosted-behaviour change, and the fixtures' second implementation is the emitted C#, not another evaluator. I corrected the README where I'd initially written otherwise.

**Verified, not assumed:** full solution 1625 tests green; the 29 SDK tests that `dotnet build` eight real generated applications green; the emitted boolean C# compiles (it did not before); backend builds; 91 platform computed tests including Budget Planner and the cohort grid still pass — so nothing was relying on the old coercion.

I left `prev()` and rollup windows unpinned deliberately — they belong with the recompute cascade, not ahead of it.

## Next

S8's remaining work is yours and still in flight (CORD2302/2303/2305/2306). **Don't start Phase 1 until it lands** — it rewrites the same files. Phases 2 (wire contract) and 3 (`node-vue`) are new files almost entirely and safe to begin any time. Say the word and I'll take the wire contract next.

content.text:
Your instinct is right about the generated path — and it already works exactly that way. But the file is doing three jobs, and only one of them is the evaluator.

## Who actually uses what

| Half | Callers |
|---|---|
| **Parser + typed AST + `Validate`** (~520 of 649 lines) | [Gate.cs:1663](oss/cordango/src/Cordango.Compiler/Definition/Gate.cs#L1663), [CordCheck.cs:87](oss/cordango/src/Cordango.Compiler/Cord/CordCheck.cs#L87), [BlueprintGate.cs:474](oss/cordango/src/Cordango.Compiler/Definition/Blueprint/BlueprintGate.cs#L474) — author-time errors — and [ComputedEmitter.cs:54](oss/cordango/src/Cordango.SourceGen.DotNetVue/Emit/ComputedEmitter.cs#L54), which walks the AST to write C# |
| **Evaluator** ([`Eval`, lines 229–354](oss/cordango/src/Cordango.Compiler/Definition/ComputedExpr.cs#L229), ~126 lines) | **exactly one** production caller: [AppDataService.cs:1677](backend/AppBuilder.Runtime/AppDataService.cs#L1677) |

`ComputedEmitter` is the only file outside `ComputedExpr.cs` that touches the AST at all (13 references), and it **never calls the evaluator**. So the standalone path is already "parse, then convert into actual code."

## Why the evaluator can't just go

The platform has no build step. `AppDataService` reads the expression string out of the stored AppDefinition, topologically sorts dependencies, and computes over a `JsonObject` — per record, at runtime. That's the hosted product: change a definition and figures recompute, no compile. Deleting the interpreter would mean the platform generates and compiles code on every definition edit, which is the standalone product wearing the platform's clothes.

So it's not "compiler needs an evaluator" — it's **the platform is an interpreter and the standalone is a compiler, and they share one language definition.** The compiler is just where the shared part lives.

## The real simplification, and it's the one that bit us

The evaluator isn't the problem. **The duplication is.** `ComputedEmitter.Binary` hand-mirrors `Eval`'s switch — two switches over the same AST that must agree, with nothing forcing it. That is precisely how `&&`-vs-`&` and the unknown-swallowing both got in, and why neither showed up until I wrote fixtures.

Worth doing, in order of value:

1. **Split the file.** `ComputedExpr` = lexer, parser, AST, `Validate` (the language). `ComputedEval` = the interpreter (the platform's runtime concern). Then the SDK can hand targets an AST without shipping an evaluator, and `node-vue` needs a TypeScript *emitter* only — no third evaluator. This is a straight file move; it changes no behaviour.

2. **Make the two switches one traversal.** A visitor over `Node` with pluggable output — one arm evaluates, one renders. A new operator then can't compile until both are handled. Bigger change, and the fixtures already catch the class of bug, so it's optional rather than urgent.

One thing I noticed while confirming this: [`EvaluateValue`](oss/cordango/src/Cordango.Compiler/Definition/ComputedExpr.cs#L110) constructs a `new Parser` and re-parses the string **on every call** — inside the recompute cascade that has already hit a performance wall twice. Caching the parsed AST per expression string looks like free speed. I haven't measured it, so treat that as a lead, not a finding.

Want me to do the split? It's mechanical, but it touches the file you have open and `ComputedEmitter.cs` that S8 is mid-edit on — so it's probably better after S8 lands, as Phase 1 of the plan already sequences.

content.text:
Facts first: the repo is genuinely public (`github.com/cordango/cordango`), `Cordango.Compiler` is 24k lines all published, and — the important one — **expressions are the only thing in the manifest that travels as an unparsed string**. Conditions already travel as structured trees (`{field, operator, value}`), which is why `ConditionEmitter` takes a `JsonNode` and never needs a parser.

That asymmetry is what's forcing your hand. Because `computed.expr` is a string, every target must parse it, so the parser must be public, and the evaluator sits in the same file.

## The move that buys you the freedom

**Lower expressions in the compiler and ship the AST in the manifest.**

```
today     manifest: { "computed": { "expr": "min(usage, cap)" } }
          target:   ComputedExpr.Parse(expr) → walk AST → emit     ← needs the parser

proposed  manifest: { "computed": { "expr": "min(usage, cap)",
                                    "tree": {"fn":"min","args":[{"field":"usage"},{"field":"cap"}]} } }
          target:   walk plain JSON → emit                          ← needs nothing
```

Targets stop depending on `Cordango.Compiler` for expressions entirely. That decouples the question "what can we close?" from "what will break?" — which is the actual blocker right now. It also makes expressions consistent with conditions instead of the exception.

## What can then close, and what can't

| Piece | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **Evaluator** ([`Eval`, 126 lines](oss/cordango/src/Cordango.Compiler/Definition/ComputedExpr.cs#L229)) | **Close it.** One production caller, the platform runtime. Clean cut. |
| **Recompute cascade, rollup windows, hops, series** | **Close.** This is the actual magic and most of it isn't written yet. |
| Parser + `Validate` | **Has to stay open** — `cordango check` validates expressions offline at author time. Close it and the OSS CLI can't tell an author their expression is wrong. |
| Semantics spec + the fixtures | **Has to stay public.** Not because of licensing, but because a target that doesn't know `min` is null-in/null-out computes different numbers. A spec is the contract, not the magic. |

There's an upside you get for free: closing the evaluator makes computed fields **match** the permissions and conditions arrangement — two independent implementations, one public hand-written fixture set, each tested in its own repo. This morning I flagged that computed was the odd one out with only one evaluator. This fixes that rather than working around it.

## The timing point

Two things are worth weighing now rather than later.

**Apache-2.0 is already out.** `ComputedExpr.cs` is public at tag 0.3.0-alpha and can't be retracted. What's still yours to place is future growth — and that's the part you're actually worried about.

**S8 is about to write the recompute cascade into the public repo.** Your own plan calls it "the hardest thing in the platform runtime," two optimisation passes to make fast. If any of it is meant to be closed, the boundary needs drawing before it lands, not after — moving it later means a public git history that already contains it.

I'd draw the line now, before S8's cascade, and start with the AST-in-manifest lowering since it's the piece that unblocks every other choice.

content.text:
The cut is clean — **the parser half has zero references to the evaluator half**. One-way dependency, evaluator → parser.

| Stays OSS (creates source code) | Moves to platform (executes) |
|---|---|
| `ComputedValueKind` — drives the emitted C# type | `ComputedValue` — a computed *value* |
| `DurationFuncs`, `MathFuncs`, `PrevFunc`, `Keywords` — the grammar | `Evaluate`, `EvaluateValue`, `Eval` |
| `Parse`, `Node`, the `Parser` class | `Divide`, `Compare`, `SameTruth`, `DifferentTruth` |
| `Validate`, `Error` — `cordango check` | `Duration`, `Bound`, `Power` |
| `LocalIdentifiers` — dependency order, used by the emitter too | |

~130 of 649 lines move. And one parser, not two: the platform consuming the OSS AST still satisfies your principle (CLI makes strings, platform makes values) without risking two grammars drifting apart.

**But there's a prerequisite you'll want to know about.** The fixtures I wrote this morning assert the *evaluator*. Move it out and OSS has no test of computed semantics at all. The fix isn't to keep the evaluator — it's that OSS should have been proving the other thing all along:

- **OSS proves**: the source code I generate computes these answers → generate a fixture app, `dotnet build` it, load it, call the computed methods.
- **Platform proves**: my executor computes these answers → its own suite, same fixtures.

Same public fixtures, two proofs, each matching its side's job. That's exactly the permissions/conditions shape. It's also the test that would have caught the `&&` bug head-on instead of by inference.

So the order has to be: **build the compile-and-run test first, then move the evaluator** — otherwise there's a window where nothing in OSS checks computed at all.

Let me size that harness before committing to it.

### Phase 0b — The OSS boundary: CLI creates source, platform executes

Tim's principle, 2026-08-22, and it cuts by **job** rather than by feature: rollups, `prev()`, hops
and series all stay on both sides — the CLI emits source for them, the platform executes them. Only
the executing half closes.

The cut is verified clean: **the parser half has zero references to the evaluator half.**

| Stays OSS — creates source code | Moves to the closed platform — executes |
|---|---|
| `ComputedValueKind` (drives the emitted C# type) | `ComputedValue` |
| `DurationFuncs`, `MathFuncs`, `PrevFunc`, `Keywords` | `Evaluate`, `EvaluateValue`, `Eval` |
| `Parse`, `Node`, the `Parser` class | `Divide`, `Compare` ×2, `SameTruth`, `DifferentTruth` |
| `Validate`, `Error` — `cordango check` offline | `Duration`, `Bound`, `Power` |
| `LocalIdentifiers` — dependency order, the emitter needs it too | (later: the recompute cascade) |

~130 of 649 lines. **One parser, not two** — the platform consuming the OSS AST satisfies the
principle without risking two grammars drifting apart, and Apache-2.0 permits closed downstream use.

#### ✅ DONE — the prerequisite

Moving the evaluator out would leave OSS with **no** test of computed semantics, because the fixtures
assert the evaluator. The fix is that OSS should have been proving the other thing all along:

- **OSS proves**: the source code I generate computes these answers.
- **Platform proves**: my executor computes these answers.

Same public fixtures, two proofs, each matching its side's job — finally the same shape as the
permission and condition fixtures.

`tests/Standalone.Tests/GeneratedComputedTests.cs` does the OSS half: it **derives** a one-entity
application from the fixture files (one computed field per case, column type from the language's own
type inference), compiles it, `dotnet build`s it, loads the assembly and invokes each generated
method against that case's record. Adding a fixture case adds a field, a method and an assertion with
nothing to keep in step by hand, and it lives outside `tests/corpus/` so it cannot disturb the corpus
counts.

Verified it actually bites: reintroducing `&&` made it fail with CS0019 naming the generated file and
line, not a vague arithmetic mismatch.

#### Remaining for the move

1. Delete the evaluator half from `ComputedExpr.cs`; add `ComputedEval` to `AppBuilder.Runtime`
   (closed), consuming `ComputedExpr.Parse`'s AST. `AppDataService.cs:1677` is the only call site.
2. Move the evaluator-side tests to the platform suite: all of `ComputedFixtureTests.Figures_match_the_fixture`
   and the `Eval`/`EvalBool` half of `Compiler.Tests/ComputedExprTests`. The fixtures themselves stay
   public — they are the specification, not the magic.
3. `ComputedFixtureTests` keeps `The_generator_writes_or_refuses_every_shape_the_fixtures_use` and the
   guard-the-guard; the semantics assertion is now `GeneratedComputedTests`.

**Timing.** Apache-2.0 is already published and cannot be retracted, so what is still yours to place
is future growth. S8 is about to write the recompute cascade — "the hardest thing in the platform
runtime", two optimisation passes — into the public repo. If it is meant to be closed, it has to land
on the closed side the first time.

### Still open in S8 (not this plan's work)

---
name: oss-boundary-cli-creates-platform-executes
description: The rule for what is open source vs closed — CLI creates source code, platform executes; cut by job, not by feature
metadata:
  type: project
---

Tim's rule for the OSS boundary, stated 2026-08-22:

> **CLI = create source code (standalone mode). Platform = execute.**

It cuts by **job**, not by feature. Rollups, `prev()`/series, cross-record hops and the cohort
primitives are not "closed features" — the CLI must emit source for all of them, and the platform
must execute all of them. Only the *executing* half closes.

**Why:** the CLI's expression handling and the platform's are different kinds of component that
happen to share a grammar. One turns an expression into strings; the other turns it into a value.
Tim's words: "the parser is meant to create strings but not execute a calculation."

**How to apply:**
- Anything the CLI needs to *emit* or to *refuse at author time* stays open: grammar, parser, AST,
  type inference (it decides the emitted C# type), `Validate`/`Error` (`cordango check` must work
  offline), and static analysis like `LocalIdentifiers` (the emitter needs dependency order too).
- Anything that *computes a value* closes: evaluator, the recompute cascade, rollup execution.
- **One grammar, not two.** The closed platform consuming the OSS parser's AST satisfies the rule
  without two grammars drifting apart. Apache-2.0 permits closed downstream use.
- **The fixtures stay public.** A spec is the contract, not the magic — a target that does not know
  `min` is null-in/null-out computes different numbers. See [[computed-unknown-is-three-valued]].
- Moving an evaluator out costs OSS its semantic coverage unless the OSS side already proves *the
  generated code* computes the right answers. `GeneratedComputedTests` does that: it derives an app
  from the fixtures, builds it, loads it, invokes the methods. Build that BEFORE the move.
- **Apache-2.0 cannot be retracted.** `github.com/cordango/cordango` is genuinely public. What is
  still placeable is future growth, so a thing meant to be closed must land closed the FIRST time.

Related: [[cord-oss-cli]], [[computed-unknown-is-three-valued]], [[calculation-plane]].

content.text:
Your rule is now the design, and I verified it cuts cleanly: **the parser half has zero references to the evaluator half.**

| Stays OSS — creates source | Moves to platform — executes |
|---|---|
| `ComputedValueKind` (drives the emitted C# type) | `ComputedValue` |
| `DurationFuncs`, `MathFuncs`, `PrevFunc`, `Keywords` | `Evaluate`, `EvaluateValue`, `Eval` |
| `Parse`, `Node`, the `Parser` class | `Divide`, `Compare`, `SameTruth`, `DifferentTruth` |
| `Validate`, `Error` — `cordango check` offline | `Duration`, `Bound`, `Power` |
| `LocalIdentifiers` — the emitter needs dependency order too | later: the recompute cascade |

~130 of 649 lines. One recommendation: **one grammar, not two.** The closed platform consuming the OSS parser's AST satisfies your rule exactly — CLI makes strings, platform makes values — without two grammars drifting apart, and Apache-2.0 permits closed downstream use.

## What I built, because the move needs it first

Pulling the evaluator out would leave OSS with **no** test of computed semantics — the fixtures I wrote this morning assert the evaluator. The fix isn't to keep it; it's that OSS should have been proving the other thing all along:

- **OSS proves**: the source code I generate computes these answers.
- **Platform proves**: my executor computes these answers.

Same public fixtures, two proofs, each matching its side's job — and it finally puts computed in the same shape as permissions and conditions.

[GeneratedComputedTests.cs](oss/cordango/tests/Standalone.Tests/GeneratedComputedTests.cs) does the OSS half: it **derives** a one-entity app from the fixture files (one computed field per case, column type from the language's own type inference), compiles it, `dotnet build`s it, loads the assembly, and invokes each generated method against that case's record. Add a fixture case and it gets a field, a method and an assertion with nothing to keep in sync — and it lives outside `tests/corpus/`, so no count tripwires.

I checked it actually bites rather than passing vacuously: reintroducing `&&` made it fail with CS0019 naming the generated file and line, then I restored the fix. Full solution green, 1632 tests, SDK builds included.

One thing to note: `created_at` is a reserved runtime base field, so fixture 03 now uses `opened_at`.

## What's left for the move

1. Delete the evaluator half from `ComputedExpr.cs`; add `ComputedEval` to `AppBuilder.Runtime`. [AppDataService.cs:1677](backend/AppBuilder.Runtime/AppDataService.cs#L1677) is the only call site.
2. Move the evaluator-side tests to the platform suite — `ComputedFixtureTests.Figures_match_the_fixture` and the `Eval`/`EvalBool` half of `ComputedExprTests`. The fixture *files* stay public.
3. `ComputedFixtureTests` keeps write-or-refuse and guard-the-guard.

I've stopped before step 1 because it edits `ComputedExpr.cs` — the file you have open — and touches the backend. Say go and I'll do it.

The timing point stands and is the part I'd weigh now: S8 is about to write the recompute cascade into the public repo. Apache-2.0 can't be retracted, so if the cascade is meant to be closed, it has to land closed the first time rather than move later.

# Computed expression fixtures

These files are the contract between the implementations of one small arithmetic.

A `computed.expr` in the definition — `total_revenue - total_costs`, `done_tasks * 100 / total_tasks`,
`min(usage, plan.cap)` — has to give the same answer everywhere it is worked out. Cordango Platform
evaluates it with `ComputedExpr.EvaluateValue`. A standalone application does not evaluate it at all:
`ComputedEmitter` turns it into a C# method at build time and the generated code computes it. Same
definition, same figures expected, two entirely different mechanisms.

That is a sharper split than the [condition fixtures](../conditions/) face, and the consequence is
worse. `ComputedEmitter` says so in its own header:

> the platform and a generated application computing different totals from one definition is the
> worst failure this project has.

A guard that answers wrongly sends one approval the wrong way and somebody notices. A total that is
quietly different in two places is found a quarter later by somebody reconciling two reports, and by
then every figure derived from it is wrong too.

So the rules are pinned here as **data**, and each implementation is asserted against the same data by
its own suite.

## The rule underneath all of them

**A blank field is zero. A figure that could not be worked out is unknown. They are not the same.**

A record with no tax has a tax of nothing, and a total that refused to add it up would be blank on
every half-filled row — so a blank NUMBER reads as zero and a blank BOOLEAN reads as false. But a
division by zero, a bound with an unknown side, a power that overflows, a duration missing an
endpoint: none of those is zero and none is an error. They are unknown, and a cap computed from an
unknown bound must not silently become no cap at all.

The distinction is easy to state and easy to lose. `min(a, b)` where both fields are blank is
**zero**, because both read as zero. `min(a, 1 / 0)` is **unknown**, because one side could not be
worked out. Most of what is pinned below is that one sentence, applied.

## What these pin, and why each one is here

1. **`01` — a blank is zero, and unknown is not.** The two kinds of missing, side by side, and what
   each does to the arithmetic around it. A blank is absorbed (`blank + 1` is `1`); an unknown
   spreads (`(1 / 0) + 1` is unknown).

2. **`02` — bounds and powers refuse to guess.** `min` and `max` are how a row states a cap on one of
   its own figures, and returning the other side when one is unknown would silently un-cap it. `pow`
   goes through `double` and comes back through a checked conversion, so overflow and NaN are
   unknown rather than an exception inside a total somebody was only reading.

3. **`03` — a duration needs both ends.** `days_between` on a record whose end date is not set is not
   a very long time and not zero. Fractional for a `datetime`, whole for a `date`.

4. **`04` — a comparison can say "cannot say".** The sharp one. Two blank number fields compare as
   `0 < 0`, which is **false** — a definite answer, because blanks are zeros. But a comparison over
   an unknown is **unknown**, which is neither true nor false. A bare `<` on two nullables in C#
   answers false for both, which would make a rule keyed on "is the balance below the threshold" fire
   on every record whose balance has not been computed yet.

5. **`05` — unknown survives boolean logic.** Written because it did not. `Compare` answered null
   carefully and then `not`, `and`, `or` and `==` coerced it straight back to false, so
   `not ((a / b) < 1)` on a blank divisor answered **true** — the evaluator had quietly decided that
   a figure nobody could work out was below the threshold. The rule is three-valued logic, which also
   keeps the answers that are still definite: unknown AND false is false whatever the unknown turns
   out to be, and unknown OR true is true.

## Format

```json
{
  "name": "what this file settles",
  "why": "why it is worth pinning",
  "fields": {
    "revenue": { "type": "decimal" },
    "months":  { "type": "integer", "required": true },
    "start":   { "type": "datetime" }
  },
  "cases": [
    {
      "why": "optional, per case",
      "record": { "revenue": 100, "months": 4 },
      "expr":   "revenue / months",
      "expect": 25
    }
  ]
}
```

`fields` declares the entity the expression is written against. It is needed and not optional: an
identifier's TYPE decides what its comparisons mean, and whether a field is `required` decides
whether the generated C# reads it as `r.X` or as `(r.X ?? 0m)`.

`record` is the record as the database holds it; a key left out is a field nobody has filled in.
`expr` is the definition's own string. `expect` is the answer every implementation must give — a JSON
number, `true`, `false`, or `null` for unknown.

## Adding one

Add a case whenever a figure surprises you, and write down in `why` what the surprise was. That
sentence is the actual deliverable — the assertion only stops the regression, while the sentence is
what stops somebody "fixing" the behaviour back.

`dotnet test oss/cordango/Cordango.slnx` picks up new files automatically.

**One suite, not two, and that is a real difference from the permission and condition fixtures.**
Those pin two independent evaluators against each other. Here there is only ONE evaluator —
`ComputedExpr` lives in `Cordango.Compiler`, and the platform runtime calls it directly rather than
carrying its own copy. So a case in these files constrains the platform through the same code it
constrains here, and changing `ComputedExpr` changes the hosted product. Run
`dotnet test backend/AppBuilder.slnx` after touching it, for the behaviour rather than for the
fixtures.

The second implementation these files exist to hold in line is not another evaluator. It is the
emitted C#.

## What these do not yet pin

**That the generated C# gives these answers when it RUNS.** `ComputedFixtureTests` asserts two things:
that the evaluator agrees with the fixture, and that `ComputedEmitter` produces something for every
shape the fixtures use rather than silently refusing it. Neither runs the emitted code.

`GeneratedArithmeticTests` does run it — it builds a real application, loads it and calls the computed
methods — but against expressions that happen to be in a corpus app rather than against these files.
Until those two meet, an expression that emits C# which compiles and returns the wrong number is
caught here only if the evaluator disagrees with the fixture, not if the emitter does.

Nor are the fixtures hand-written from an implementation. They are written from the rules above, which
is the same discipline the [permission fixtures](../permissions/) state and for the same reason:
recording would make one implementation the definition of correct and enshrine its bugs as the
contract the other has to match.

input.new_string:
## How each side is held to them

- **`GeneratedComputedTests`** (this repository) derives a one-entity application from these very
  files — one computed field per case — compiles it with `dotnet build`, loads the assembly and
  invokes each generated method. It is the only test that can say what the generated arithmetic
  actually answers, because a generated application carries no expression, no parser and no fixture.
- **`ComputedFixtureTests`** (this repository) checks that the emitter produces something for every
  shape rather than silently refusing it. Emitting is not compiling: a refused expression leaves a
  column permanently empty, which looks exactly like a column whose inputs are empty.
- **`ComputedFixtureTests`** (the platform) drives the same cases through `ComputedEval`.

The fixtures are hand-written from the rules above, never recorded from either side — the same
discipline the [permission fixtures](../permissions/) state, and for the same reason: recording would
make one implementation the definition of correct and enshrine its bugs as the contract the other has
to match.

## What these still do not pin

`prev()` and rollup windows. Both need an ordered series or a set of related records rather than one
row, so a case for them needs a different harness than a single record and a single expression. They
belong with the recompute cascade.

content.text:
Done. The evaluator is out of the open-source compiler.

## What moved

**OSS `ComputedExpr.cs`: 649 → 489 lines.** Gone: `ComputedValue`, `Evaluate`, `EvaluateValue`, `Eval`, `Divide`, `Compare` ×2, `SameTruth`, `DifferentTruth`, `Duration`, `Bound`, `Power`. Kept: the grammar vocabulary, `Parse`, the AST, `Validate`/`Error`, `LocalIdentifiers`. I rewrote the class doc — it used to say "parsing and evaluation use the same AST," which is no longer true.

**New, closed: [ComputedEval.cs](backend/AppBuilder.Runtime/ComputedEval.cs)** — the evaluator plus `ComputedValue`, consuming the AST `ComputedExpr.Parse` returns. One grammar, two consumers. [AppDataService.cs:1677](backend/AppBuilder.Runtime/AppDataService.cs#L1677) was the only call site.

**Tests followed the code.** The 12 hand-written evaluator tests and the fixture-driven one are now `AppBuilder.Runtime.Tests/ComputedEvalTests.cs` and `ComputedFixtureTests.cs`. OSS keeps the 12 parse/type-inference tests, write-or-refuse, and guard-the-guard. `GeneratedArithmeticTests` no longer compares against an evaluator — its `InlineData` is the expectation now, and `GeneratedComputedTests` carries the cross-implementation proof.

## The rule is mechanical now, not remembered

I added `OssBoundaryTests.The_open_source_compiler_parses_expressions_but_does_not_evaluate_them` alongside the existing dependency-direction tests. It reflects over the loaded `Cordango.Compiler` and fails if any public static `Eval*` reappears on `ComputedExpr`, while asserting `Parse`/`Validate`/`LocalIdentifiers` are still there.

That felt worth doing because the natural place for someone to add "just a small helper that works out what this comes to" is right next to the parser — and Apache-2.0 can't be taken back once it ships.

## Verified

- **OSS**: 1615 green. Counts dropped exactly as expected (Compiler −12, Standalone −5 — the moved tests), and nothing in `src/` or `tests/` references the evaluator any more.
- **Platform**: 515 non-database tests green, including Budget Planner, the cohort grid, and both fixture suites. `OssBoundaryTests` 4/4.
- The Postgres store tests fail refusing at `127.0.0.1:5432` — the db container isn't running. Pre-existing, unrelated to this, and I didn't start it since that's your call.

I also corrected the fixtures README: it said "one suite, not two," which was accurate this morning and wrong after the move. There are genuinely two implementations held to those files now — the emitted arithmetic and the platform evaluator — which is the arrangement you wanted all along.

**S8's recompute cascade is the next thing this rule governs, and it hasn't landed yet.** That's the one still worth deciding before it's written.

content.content:
This is the PRIMARY distribution channel and the tool package is the convenience one. Cordango is
    an application language, not a .NET product: somebody authoring a definition to generate a Go or
    React target should never be asked to install a .NET SDK to do it, and the first-party target
    being .NET is an accident of which generator was written first.

    Every property here is a decision:

      PublishSingleFile          one file to download, one file to put on PATH. The schemas and the
                                 whole scaffold are embedded resources and survive bundling — proven
                                 by generating an application with the published binary, not assumed.

      EnableCompressionInSingleFile  39 MB instead of about 75. Costs a few tens of milliseconds of
                                 decompression at startup, once.

      InvariantGlobalization     no libicu on the target machine. A self-contained .NET application
                                 otherwise refuses to start on Alpine and on slim images, with an
                                 error naming a library nobody installed on purpose. Safe here
                                 because this codebase compares Ordinal and formats InvariantCulture
                                 throughout — verified rather than assumed: the same definition built
                                 with and without ICU produces byte-identical output.

      DebugType none             the release asset is the binary and nothing else. Symbols for a
                                 stack trace come from the .snupkg the NuGet channel publishes.

    Not here, deliberately: PublishTrimmed and PublishAot. Both would cut the size a lot and both
    break reflection, and JsonSchema.Net is exactly the kind of dependency that fails at RUN time
    rather than at publish. Worth trying behind the compile-every-corpus-app test, later, on purpose.
  -->
  <PropertyGroup Condition="'$(PublishSingleFile)' == 'true'">
    <EnableCompressionInSingleFile>true</EnableCompressionInSingleFile>
    <InvariantGlobalization>true</InvariantGlobalization>
    <DebugType>none</DebugType>
    <SatelliteResourceLanguages>en</SatelliteResourceLanguages>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <!--
    THIS IS A .NET TOOL: `dotnet tool install -g Cordango.Cli`, then the command is `cordango`.

    The first distribution channel, and the cheapest by a distance — the same pack-and-push the other
    packages already use, no signing, no notarization, no tap or bucket repository to maintain. It
    needs the .NET SDK on the machine, which for this audience is close to free: somebody generating a
    standalone application gets an ASP.NET Core project out, and is going to need the SDK to work
    on it.

    It is not the LAST channel. A self-contained binary per platform, behind Homebrew on macOS, Scoop
    on Windows and an install script on Linux, is what reaches everybody else, and this project file
    already carries the PublishSingleFile intent for it.

    THE THREE PROJECT REFERENCES SHIP INSIDE THIS PACKAGE, not as dependencies on it. A tool package

content.text:
Good — we were talking about two different Roslyn APIs, and the distinction changes the answer. Let me be precise about what each one actually buys, because it affects whether this is worth doing.

## The correction that matters

`SyntaxFactory` builds a **syntax** tree. It would **not** have caught the `&&` bug. `a && b` is perfectly valid C# syntax — `CS0019` is a *semantic* error that only appears once a `CSharpCompilation` with real references type-checks it. So "use Roslyn to build the tree" and "use Roslyn to verify the output" are separate things, and only the second catches the class of bug we hit today.

Worth knowing: **the semantic gate already exists.** `GeneratedApplicationTests` runs `dotnet build` over 8 real corpus apps, and `GeneratedComputedTests` now does the same for every fixture case. That's a full compile with real references — stronger than anything an in-process Roslyn check would give, and it caught the reintroduced `&&` when I tested it. What was missing was never the mechanism; it was **coverage**, because no corpus app had a boolean computed field. That hole is closed.

So the safety argument for SyntaxFactory is weaker than it looks. The ergonomic argument is real, though.

## Where `SyntaxFactory` genuinely wins

| Emitter | Fit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `ComputedEmitter` (207 ln), `ConditionEmitter` (152 ln) | **Strong** | Tree→tree mapping. **Precedence comes from the tree structure**, so you can't silently change arithmetic by missing a paren. Today it brute-forces parens around every binary op — safe, but noisier output than needed. `SyntaxFactory.Literal(1.5m)` also kills the hand-rolled `Literal()`. |
| `EntityEmitter`, `ConfigurationEmitter` (297 ln) | Neutral | Mechanical property/fluent lists. Verbose in SyntaxFactory, no safety gain over `dotnet build`. |
| `BackendEmitter` (662 ln), `MigrationEmitter` (272 ln), `WorkflowEmitter` (256 ln) | **Poor** | Whole classes with XML doc comments. Roslyn trivia is genuinely unpleasant, and this is boilerplate that reads better as a template. |
| `WebEmitter` (651 ln), `Scaffold`, `SeedEmitter` | **N/A** | Vue SFCs and JSON. Roslyn cannot touch any of it. |

Roughly 360 lines are a strong fit; ~1200 are neutral-to-poor; ~1200 are out of scope entirely.

## The wrinkle that actually matters for your plan

**ts-morph is a Node library, and the CLI is C#.** So for a TypeScript target you get three choices, and none is free:

- Shell out to Node at generation time — breaks the stated promise that the 39 MB binary needs nothing installed. It'd need Node instead of .NET.
- Write a TS syntax builder in C# — that's the string problem again with more ceremony.
- **Make `node-vue` an out-of-process generator written in Node**, using ts-morph natively. That's exactly the stdin/stdout protocol `Contracts.cs` reserves and `Targets.cs` anticipates — reserved, never built.

That third option is coherent and it means each target uses its own language's real tooling. But it **reverses the call you made earlier** ("c# generator should run everywhere so we can just use it"). Your fragility concern and your multi-language goal are pulling toward the same place, and it's not where we landed.

One honest caveat either way: **the Vue half stays string-built regardless.** There's no AST-builder for `.vue` SFCs — `@vue/compiler-sfc` parses, it doesn't construct. The real gate there is running `vue-tsc` / `npm run build`, which is the test gap I flagged earlier and still isn't closed.

Cost note: Roslyn adds roughly 5–8 MB compressed to a binary whose "one file, about 39 MB" is a stated selling point. I haven't measured it — that's an estimate, not a finding.

content.text:
You haven't misinterpreted — but here's the thing: **you already have that AST, and it already works exactly the way you're describing.**

`ComputedExpr.Node` is a language-agnostic source AST. Look at what its operators actually are:

```
BinaryNode("and", left, right)     ← Cordango's spelling, not C#'s
FunctionNode("min", left, right)   ← not Math.Min, not Math.min
DurationNode("days_between", …)
PrevNode(field, seed)
```

Nothing in it is C#. `ComputedEmitter` is a *renderer* over that AST — it turns `"and"` into `&`, `"min"` into `Calc.Min(…)`. A TypeScript renderer walks the same nodes and emits `&&`-with-null-guards and `calc.min(…)`. Conditions are the same story: a JSON tree, with `ConditionEmitter` rendering it.

So the layer you're reaching for exists:

```
AppDefinition (JSON)        ← describes the app          ✅ exists
   │
   ├─ Condition tree (JSON)  ← language-agnostic         ✅ exists
   └─ ComputedExpr.Node      ← language-agnostic         ✅ exists
        │
        ├─ C# renderer   (ComputedEmitter)               ✅ exists
        └─ TS renderer   (node-vue)                      ← the only new thing needed
```

## Where it stops, and why

The instinct fails one level up. **Statements, declarations and types do not survive the trip**, and the sharpest proof is `money`:

C# has `decimal` — base-10, exact, the right type for money. TypeScript's `number` is an IEEE-754 double; `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3`. A TS target has to pick something else entirely: decimal.js, or integer cents, or strings. That choice changes **the shape of every arithmetic expression around it** — `a + b` becomes `a.plus(b)`. That isn't a rendering decision a shared AST can defer; it's a design decision per target, and it reaches back into how the expression renderer works.

Same for the rest: C# properties vs TS fields, nullable value types vs `| undefined`, `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` vs a Prisma schema DSL (which isn't even code). Push the AST up to that level and you get one of two known failures — an AST that's secretly C#-shaped and the TS renderer fights it, or one so abstract every target needs escape hatches. And either way the output stops looking idiomatic, which breaks the standalone promise of "an ordinary application, not one only our toolchain understands."

| Layer | Language-agnostic? | Status |
|---|---|---|
| App definition (JSON) | Yes | ✅ exists |
| Condition tree | Yes | ✅ exists |
| **Expression AST** | **Yes** | **✅ exists — `ComputedExpr.Node`** |
| Statements, declarations, types | **No** — `decimal` alone breaks it | per-target |
| Framework wiring (EF config, controllers, Prisma) | **No** — not even the same shape | per-target |

## What that means for the fragility worry

It splits cleanly, and mostly in your favour:

- **Expressions** — the place where a wrong answer is catastrophic and silent — are *already* tree-driven, not string-spliced. Precedence comes from tree structure. What remains is literal formatting and type mistakes like `&&`-on-`bool?`, and the latter is caught by `dotnet build` over 8 corpus apps plus the fixture app.
- **Program structure** — genuinely string-built, genuinely more fragile, but fully covered by that same compile gate.
- **Vue** — string-built with *no gate at all*. A generated `.vue` with a syntax error still ships green today.

So the one place with real, uncovered fragility is the Vue emitter, and no AST library fixes it — `@vue/compiler-sfc` parses SFCs, it doesn't construct them. The fix there is running the actual toolchain.

My recommendation, in order of value per unit of work: **close the Vue gap** (`npm ci && npm run build` in the generated-app suite), then when `node-vue` starts, write the TS renderer over the *existing* `ComputedExpr.Node` rather than inventing a new IR. Roslyn `SyntaxFactory` stays optional — it'd tidy the C# renderer, but it buys no correctness the compile gate isn't already providing.

Want me to close the Vue gap now? It's contained, and it's the only place currently shipping unverified code.

+    /// <summary>Parts joined and indented as one block, for the hole in a template that stands on

+    public static string Block(IEnumerable<string> parts, int indent, string separator = "\n\n") =>
+        Indent(string.Join(separator, parts), indent);

content.text:
Pilot done, and it's a clean result.

## Proof

**All 2023 generated files byte-identical**, before vs after, across the whole corpus. Full suite green — 1615 tests, including the 43-second pass that actually `dotnet build`s 8 real applications plus the fixture app, so the emitted entity classes genuinely compile.

## What changed

You can now read the emitter as the file it produces. Nineteen `source.Line(...)` calls became one template with three holes. The escaping went away too — this:

```csharp
source.Line("[JsonPropertyName(\"id\")] public string Id { get; set; } = \"\";");
```

is now literally the line it emits, backslashes and all gone.

A subtler win: `EmitField(Source source, EntityModel entity, FieldModel field)` became `Property(FieldModel field)`. It no longer takes the buffer or the entity — it takes a field and returns a string. Pieces compose instead of mutating shared state, which is the property that actually makes this scale.

## The honest costs

**The file got slightly longer** — 163 → 176 lines, plus 26 for the shared `Code` helper. Templates aren't automatically shorter; they're clearer. If you were hoping for less code, this isn't it.

**There's one sharp edge, and you'd hit it 20+ times converting the rest.** C# strips the common margin from a raw string's *literal* lines only — an interpolated block lands at column zero no matter how neatly the template around it is laid out. That's what `Code.Block(members, indent: 4)` exists for. It's easy once you know, invisible until you don't, and it's the reason I'd want that helper in place before converting anything else.

**Repetition needs a list, not a loop.** The `foreach` that appended to a buffer became "build a `List<string>`, splice it as one block." That's the pattern for every emitter with a variable member count, and it's why I picked this file for the pilot rather than the `Controller` method I showed you earlier — that one is pure fixed structure and would have flattered the approach.

## My read

It's better, but modestly so on one small file. The case gets stronger with size: `BackendEmitter` has 223 of these calls and `WebEmitter` 112, and those are where brace bookkeeping actually goes wrong. `WebEmitter` is also the one with no compile gate at all, so authoring clarity there is worth more than anywhere else.

Your call on scope. Options as I see them, roughly ascending: stop here and keep it as a proven pattern for new emitters; convert `WebEmitter` next (highest risk, no gate, and it proves the approach on Vue rather than C#); or work through all the C# emitters. I'd suggest `WebEmitter` next if you want to continue — the diff technique makes each conversion provably safe, so they can be done one at a time whenever it suits.

# Expenses

An employee files an expense claim. An approver approves or declines it. Once approved, somebody
marks it reimbursed.

content.content:
# Cordango examples

Four complete Cordango applications, as source you can clone, read, change and build.

> Status: pre-alpha. These track the App Definition schema in
> [cordango/cordango](https://github.com/cordango/cordango) and will move while it settles.

Each directory is a real workspace, not a snippet. What you see is what an author writes: one file
per aggregate, an entity here, a lifecycle there, a role, a screen. No compiled App Definition is
checked in, because that is the output of the toolchain rather than the thing a person edits.

```
cd expenses
cordango check                        # parse, lower and validate. No model, no database.
cordango inspect                      # what is in here
cordango check --target standalone    # can this be generated as an application you own?

cordango build --target standalone --out generated --allow-incomplete
cd generated && docker compose up --build
```

`--allow-incomplete` is needed today and says so out loud. The standalone generator does not yet
emit workflows, computed fields or command guards, and rather than shipping an application that
looks finished it refuses the build until you say you know. Every gap is listed in the generated
README and recorded in `cordango.build.json`, so a partial build can never pass for a complete one
later.

Then open <http://localhost:8080>: the first screen asks you to create the administrator account.
There is no default password and none is generated for you.

## The examples

| Example | Entities | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`expenses/`](expenses) | 1 | The smallest complete application, and the one to read first. An approval lifecycle, and three roles that see genuinely different things. |
| [`time-off/`](time-off) | 1 | Absence requests with a manager approval step, a team schedule, and a duration the application works out for itself. |
| [`task-manager/`](task-manager) | 5 | Projects, tasks, subtasks and milestones, with rollups that let a parent count its children. Read this one for computed fields. |
| [`room-booking/`](room-booking) | 4 | Rooms, bookings, attendees, and a policy entity that holds the rules instead of hard-coding them. |

## Reading one

Start with `apps/<name>/app.cordango.yaml`, which names the application and fixes the order things
appear in. Then:

```
entities/           what the application stores, one file per entity
workflows/          lifecycles (a record's states and the moves between them) and automations
roles/              who may read, write and run what
views/collections/  a table, board or calendar over one entity
views/screens/      a page, assembled from views and blocks
views/entities/     one record's detail, peek and form
```

## Contributing

An improvement here reaches everyone using the example, in either environment. Clearer labels, more
realistic permissions, a state a lifecycle is missing, a screen that reads better: all welcome.

Two things to check before opening a pull request:

```
cordango check --app <name>
cordango check --app <name> --target standalone
```

The first asks whether it is a valid Cordango application. The second asks the narrower question of
whether the standalone generator can also build it. A standalone build is one application, so
anything that depends on other installed applications is reported rather than silently dropped.

## Where these came from

Each was imported from the conformance corpus in the compiler repository using `cordango import`,
which turns an App Definition back into source. That corpus stays where it is, because the test
suite is pinned to it and it must not drift. These copies are the ones meant for people to read,
and they are allowed to grow.

## License

Apache-2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

# Budget Planner

Build an investor-ready financial plan: named scenarios, a usage-based price list, customer growth
and churn, hiring by team, cost lines, funding rounds, and a cash balance that runs month by month
until it tells you how much runway is left.

It is by a distance the largest application here — sixteen entities and seventy-three computed
fields — and it exists because it is the one that could not be built at all until the calculation
plane was. Read the others first. Read this one when you want to know how far the language goes.

## What to look at

**`entities/period.cordango.yaml` and `entities/scenario.cordango.yaml`** are where the arithmetic
lives. A period's figures are computed from its own row, from its parent scenario, and from the
period *before it* — a running cash balance is `prev(cash_at_end, scenario.starting_cash) +
net_cash_movement`, which is the recurrence a spreadsheet writes as `=B26+C24-C25` and which no
expression over a single record can say. That one primitive is why this application is expressible.

**`entities/cohort_month.cordango.yaml`** is the other half. Customers arrive in a month and decay
over the months after it, so revenue in any period is a sum over every cohort still alive. The grid
is built by a workflow rather than modelled by hand, because the number of rows depends on the plan
length.

**`entities/revenue_plan.cordango.yaml`** carries the pricing. Every per-plan difference is a NUMBER
on the plan row rather than a branch, because an expression cannot read a select — so a base fee, a
cap multiplier and a price per app-user are three columns, and the same formula serves every plan.

**`views/screens/projection.cordango.yaml`** is the payoff: recognised revenue and cash collected
side by side, which are not the same number and are the two an investor asks about.

**`roles/`** has three, and the interesting one is `viewer` — an investor or a board member who may
read a scenario and change nothing in it.

## Running it

```
cordango check                        # is this a valid Cordango application?
cordango check --target standalone    # can the standalone generator build it?

cordango build --target standalone --out generated --allow-incomplete
cd generated && docker compose up --build
```

## What does not build yet

This is the honest part, and it is why `--allow-incomplete` is not optional here. The build reports
**seventy-three gaps** and writes every one of them into the generated README and into
`cordango.build.json`:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **48 × CORD2305** | computed fields. 31 are rollups over other records, 17 read something outside their own row. The columns exist and stay empty. |
| **18 × CORD2301** | screen blocks the generator does not draw yet — `create`, `repeat`, `chip`, `tiles`, `settings`, `action`. Each leaves a card on the page saying so. |
| **5 × CORD2303** | `createRecord` and `updateRecord` effects on commands. The command runs and moves the record; the effect does not fire. |
| **2 × CORD2102** | `history` blocks. Record history is a platform feature — a standalone application keeps no business audit trail, so this one will not arrive in a later release. |

So what you get today is the data model, the API, the permissions, the commands and most of the
screens. **What you do not get is the arithmetic** — which, in a budget planner, is the application.
It compiles, it runs, and every figure that depends on a rollup or on another record is blank.

That is the point of building it now: the gaps are a list somebody can read rather than a wall, and
this application is the acceptance case for closing them.

# Budget Planner

A Cordango workspace. One repository is one installation: the apps under `apps/` share
People, Organizations and Calendar, and they are built, reviewed and deployed together.

```
cordango check        # parse, lower and validate every app
cordango inspect      # what is in here
cordango build        # write .cordango/build/<app>/
```

The first app is in [`apps/budget_planner`](apps/budget_planner). Change it or delete it.

**One workspace holds many apps.** `cordango add app <name>` adds another under `apps/`; they
share People, Organizations and Calendar, reference each other's records, and are checked,
built and deployed together. `cordango new` is only for creating the workspace itself.

**People, Organizations and Calendar are already there.** They are core apps the platform
provides — `core_people`, `core_organizations`, `core_calendar`. Point at them instead of
declaring your own company or contact entity:

```
cordango inspect                          # lists them, with their entity keys
cordango vocabulary core organizations    # what one of them holds
```

A field pointing at one is `type: reference` with `targetApp: core_organizations` and
`target: organization`. Nothing about this needs an instance or a login.

Semantic source lives in `.cordango.yaml` files, one per aggregate — an entity, a lifecycle, a role, a
screen. They are the source of truth. `.cordango/` (with the leading dot) is build output and is
not committed.
