Done. `oss/examples/budget-planner/` exists, follows the documented convention (imported with `cordango import`, like the other four), and **both halves build**.

## Where we are

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| `cordango import` | 93 source files, checks ok |
| `cordango check` | ok |
| `cordango check --target standalone` | 2 × `history` block — platform-only, will never build here |
| `cordango build --allow-incomplete` | **194 files written**, 73 gaps recorded |
| `dotnet build generated/api` | **0 errors** (1 pre-existing runtime warning) |
| `npm run build` in `generated/web` | **clean** — 682 modules → `api/wwwroot` |

That's the first time the Vue output has been built at all, and it passed. Doesn't close the gap — there's still no automated gate — but it's evidence the emitter isn't producing garbage.

## The 73 gaps

```
48 × CORD2305   computed fields   31 rollups over other records
                                  17 reading outside their own row
18 × CORD2301   screen blocks     create, repeat, chip, tiles, settings, action
 5 × CORD2303   effects           createRecord, updateRecord on commands
 2 × CORD2102   history blocks    platform-only, permanent
```

## The honest headline

**It compiles, it runs, and the arithmetic is missing.** You get the data model, the API, permissions, commands, migrations and most screens. What you don't get is 48 of the 73 computed fields — every rollup and every cross-record read is a column that exists and stays blank.

For a budget planner, that *is* the application. Which makes it a good thing to have built now: this is exactly the S8 acceptance case, and the gap list is a to-do rather than a wall. What landed this morning — the three-valued logic, the fixtures, the compile-and-run test — covers single-row arithmetic. The 48 that are missing are the rollup/cascade half, which is the work that hasn't started.

Two notes: `generated/` is gitignored per the repo's convention, so only the 93 source files and the README are new to git. And I added the row to the examples index (`Four` → `Five`).

Want me to `docker compose up` and actually drive it in a browser? That's the next thing that would tell you something the build can't — the `run` skill would drive it and screenshot the projection screen, where the blank columns will be very visible.

content.text:
Found it — and it's better news than the diagnostic implies.

## Why the `create` block isn't emitted

It's simply one of the block kinds `WebEmitter`'s switch doesn't cover yet. The schema defines **41** block kinds; the emitter handles **18**:

```
handled   card chart child columns field fields grid hub process progress
          row section stack stat table tabs text view

not yet   action answers avatar board calendar cell chip control create
          externalEmbed filterbar form gantt intake orgchart repeat
          settings split tiles timeline widgets            (21)

never     history relatedApps                              (2 — platform-only)
```

The target's capability declaration says it *supports* `create` — which is correct, a standalone app can obviously have a New button. The emitter just hasn't caught up. That's the whole distinction between `CORD2301` ("not generated yet") and `CORD2102` ("never coming"), and it's why they print differently in the README.

## But on this page it's cosmetic, not a hole

The machinery is already built and already wired. [`RecordDialog.vue`](oss/cordango/src/Cordango.Standalone/Templates/web/src/blocks/RecordDialog.vue) does creation properly — `isNew`, `createRecord`, and it filters out system, read-only and `hideOnCreate` fields so nobody gets an approver box on a creation form. And `ViewBlock` already imports it:

```vue
create: { type: Boolean, default: true },
...
<v-btn v-if="create" prepend-icon="mdi-plus" @click="editing = {}">New</v-btn>
```

So `<ViewBlock view="scenarios_table" />` on that page **already renders a New button and a working create dialog**. The `create` block the author put beside it is a second, explicit affordance — a prominent call-to-action rather than the table's own small button. Only that explicit one is missing.

So the page works. You can create a scenario. What you lose is the placement the author asked for, and you get a grey card saying so instead.

That pattern holds for several of the 18 `CORD2301`s here — `chip`, `tiles`, `repeat` are presentational. It does **not** hold for the 48 computed fields, which are genuine holes with nothing standing in for them.

Worth noting for the emitter backlog: `create` looks cheap precisely *because* `RecordDialog` exists and `hub` already imports it. It's wiring an existing component into one more switch case, not new machinery — unlike `form` or `intake`, which need real work.

=== template ===
# Everything {{AppName}} needs to run, on one machine.
#
# Two services and two volumes. The database version is pinned rather than floating on `latest`,
# because a Postgres major upgrade is a decision to make deliberately on a Tuesday morning and not
# one to discover after a `docker compose pull`.

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17.5-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: {{AppKey}}
      POSTGRES_USER: {{AppKey}}
      # Defaulted so that `docker compose up` works with no setup at all. It is safe HERE and only
      # here: this service publishes no port, so the only thing that can reach the database is the
      # app container on this compose network. Set DB_PASSWORD in .env before you put this anywhere
      # real — and certainly before you add a `ports:` mapping to this service.
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-cordango-local-only}
    volumes:
      - db:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U {{AppKey}}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20

  app:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      # The application migrates its own schema at startup, so it needs a database that is ready to
      # answer rather than merely a container that has been created.
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      ConnectionStrings__Database: "Host=db;Port=5432;Database={{AppKey}};Username={{AppKey}};Password=${DB_PASSWORD:-cordango-local-only}"
      # The generated demo dataset, loaded into empty tables only. Once there are rows this does
      # nothing, so it is safe to leave on — set SEED=false to skip it entirely.
      Seed__Enabled: ${SEED:-true}
      Seed__Date: ${SEED_DATE:-}

      # The first administrator, for an UNATTENDED start. Empty by default, and empty is the
      # normal case: the application then has no account at all, and the first screen anybody
      # reaches asks them to create one. That is how a person gets in without being handed a
      # password somebody or something else chose.
      #
      # Set both anywhere the first request will not be yours — the account exists before the
      # application accepts anything, and the setup screen never appears. After an administrator
      # exists these are ignored, and they never reset a password.
      Admin__Email: ${ADMIN_EMAIL:-}
      Admin__Password: ${ADMIN_PASSWORD:-}
    ports:
      - "${PORT:-8080}:8080"
    volumes:
      # Everything this application must not lose when the container is replaced: uploaded files,
      # and the key ring that its session and antiforgery cookies are protected with. The whole
      # directory rather than just the uploads, because a container REBUILDS its own filesystem —
      # keys written inside it are gone on the next `docker compose up`, and the symptom is that
      # everybody is signed out and the first POST from an already-open tab is refused as a stale
      # token.
      - data:/appdata

volumes:
  db:
  data:

content.text:
Here's where things stand.

## Docker compose — fixed

The collision was worse than a name clash. Compose names the project after the **directory**, and every app builds into one called `generated` — so two apps shared containers, network, *and the `generated_db` volume*. The second `docker compose up` was attaching to the first app's database.

```yaml
name: budget-planner
services:
  db:
    container_name: budget-planner-db
  app:
    container_name: budget-planner-app
```

Pinned by a regression test. One correction to your spec: there are **two** services, not three — the `app` container serves the API *and* the built SPA (vite outputs into `api/wwwroot`), so there's no separate `api` container. I also noted in `.env.example` that the second app needs a different `PORT`, since both default to 8080 and only one can bind.

## Gaps closed: 73 → 35

| | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| `CORD2301` screen blocks | 18 | **0** |
| `CORD2303` command effects | 5 | **0** |
| `CORD2305` computed — hops | 15 | **0** |
| `CORD2305` computed — rollups | 31 | 31 |
| `CORD2305` computed — `prev()` | 2 | 2 |
| `CORD2102` history | 2 | 2 (permanent) |

**Screen blocks** — six new leaf components (`CreateButton`, `BlockChip`, `TilesBlock`, `SettingsBlock`, `ActionButton`, `RepeatBlock`) plus a `repeat` case that emits a scoped slot, so `record` inside a repeat means the repeated row. Added a `cordango:records-changed` signal so a create button refreshes lists elsewhere on the page.

**Command effects** — commands now carry the same `WorkflowEffect` types workflows do and run through the same runner. I generalised `WorkflowRunner` from "workflow" to a source label rather than writing a second effect implementation, so `createRecord` means one thing.

**Hops** — `segment.mature_active_users` now resolves. The computed methods stay pure functions; a generated `Refs` holder is loaded by the hook and passed in:

```csharp
public static decimal? ActiveUsers(LifecycleStep r, Refs refs) =>
    (((decimal?)refs.Segment?.MatureActiveUsers ?? 0m) * ((decimal?)refs.Point?.UserAdoption ?? 0m));
```

**Verified**: 1616 tests green (including `dotnet build` of 8 corpus apps + the fixture app), the budget planner's API compiles, and its Vue builds — 688 modules.

## Why I've stopped here rather than starting the rollups

The 31 rollups aren't more of the same. They need the **recompute cascade**, and `Cordango.Standalone` has no rollup concept at all — grep finds nothing. That means building: the aggregate query, an after-write hook on every *child* that recomputes its parent, a depth guard against parents that feed each other, and ordering between rollup fields and the expressions that read them.

Your own plan calls this "the hardest thing in the platform runtime," two optimisation passes to make fast. I'd be starting it at the end of a long session, and a half-built cascade that silently recomputes the wrong set is worse than a column that's honestly empty — which is what the 31 `CORD2305`s currently say.

I'd rather do it as its own pass, starting with the 15 simple parent rollups (`sum` up a reference) before the 16 windowed/matched ones. Say the word and I'll begin.

content.text:
You're right. I over-estimated, and the reason is worth naming: I imported the *platform's* constraint. The platform is an interpreter — it meets a definition it has never seen at runtime, so it needs a general cascade with cycle detection and coalescing. That's what hit the recompute wall.

**The generator knows the whole graph at build time.** Across the entire corpus it's acyclic and shallow — max depth 2:

```
scenario ← period ← {acquisition, cohort_month, cost_line, funding_round, hiring_line, revenue_stream}
scenario ← {acquisition, cost_line, funding_round, hiring_line, period}
```

So there's no engine to write. The generator topologically sorts the entity graph once, refuses loudly if it ever finds a cycle (a diagnostic, not a runtime guard), and emits a **straight-line call chain**. That's the project's own doctrine from the APIGenerator assessment: *"machinery that exists to answer a question at startup that we answer at generation time."*

And the rollups themselves really are just queries. Even the windowed ones I'd flagged as hard:

```json
{"entity":"hiring_line","via":"scenario","match":"scenario","op":"sum","field":"monthly_cost",
 "window":{"from":"start_month","to":"end_month","against":"start_date"}}
```
→
```csharp
r.PayrollCost = await db.Set<HiringLine>()
    .Where(x => x.Scenario == r.Scenario)                                    // match
    .Where(x => x.StartDate >= r.StartMonth && x.StartDate <= r.EndMonth)    // window
    .SumAsync(x => (decimal?)x.MonthlyCost, ct);
```

`match` is a WHERE, `window` is two more. That's 29 of the 31.

## So the plan is

1. **Order the graph at generation time.** Extend the existing `Ordered()` so rollups and expressions interleave by dependency — an expression that reads a rollup comes after it. Refuse on a cycle.
2. **Emit `{Entity}Rollups.ApplyAsync(r, db, ct)`** — one query per rollup, then the existing pure `Apply` for the expressions that read them.
3. **Emit a cascade hook per child** — `IAfterCreate/Update/Delete`, recomputing the parents that child affects, in the generator's static order. For `via` it's a foreign key; for `match`+`window` it's a query. Both mechanical.

That's 29 gaps. Straight-line, no runtime discovery.

## The two that genuinely aren't queries

`prev()` — `cash_end = prev(cash_end, scenario.starting_cash) + net_cash_movement`. Each row reads the row before it, so it's an ordered fold over the series, not an aggregate. Different shape, but small and self-contained: order the periods, walk them once.

## One thing I won't hide

The cascade will be O(children) per write — editing one `hiring_line` recomputes every period in that scenario. For a budget planner that's 24–60 rows, fine. It's exactly where the platform eventually hit its wall, and your own memory records that **in-memory timings hid that wall by two orders of magnitude**. So I'll build it simple and correct first, and measure against Postgres rather than against a passing test.

Want me to start? I'd do the 15 simple `via` rollups end to end first — emit, cascade, compile, run — so the shape is proven before the 14 windowed ones land on top of it.
